title: Nearly 90% in Yolanda mass grave identified
content:
Nearly 90% in Yolanda mass grave identified
TACLOBAN CITY, Philippines — After more than a decade of having nameless crosses in a lonely field, victims buried in the Yolanda mass grave may finally have their names in their resting places.
Following the completion of DNA analysis, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Regional Office VIII has announced a breakthrough: nearly 90 percent of the victims buried in the mass grave have been identified.
Results of the disaster victim identification are expected to be released on Nov. 8, before the 13th anniversary of Super Typhoon Yolanda’s onslaught, according to NBI Region VIII director Jeremy Lotoc.
For 13 years, over 2,200 deceased have lain in the mass grave at the Holy Cross Memorial in Barangay Basper, Tacloban City.
“These are not just numbers. They are mothers, fathers, children, whose families have been waiting for 13 long years to know where their loved ones are,” Lotoc said.
Once released, the disaster victim identification results will be turned over to Tacloban officials, aiding in the restructuring of the crosses and tombs.
“From nameless graves to named memories – after 13 years of waiting, grieving and hoping, justice and closure may finally come for the thousands who perished in one of the country’s darkest days,” Lotoc added.
About 6,300 people, mostly in Eastern Visayas, died in the onslaught of Yolanda, marking it as one of the deadliest natural calamities in Philippine history.
Tacloban was its ground zero, wherein more than 2,000 residents were killed by the super typhoon and its devastating storm surges that swallowed entire communities.
Thirteen years later, the mass grave in Barangay Basper remains more than just a burial ground – it stands as a sacred place of remembrance, a silent witness to the lives lost and the pain that still lingers.
For families mourning relatives who were never found or identified, the site is where prayers are whispered, candles are lit and memories are kept alive.
Each name remembered is a promise that even after over a decade, Tacloban will never forget.

title: DOH advises public against relying solely on water filters
content:
DOH advises public against relying solely on water filters
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Health (DOH) has advised the public against relying entirely on water filtration devices to ensure safe drinking water as the country prepares for the effects of the impending super El Niño.
The DOH recommended pretreating raw water containing debris, organic matter and suspended solids to prevent filtration systems from getting clogged and ensure their effectiveness.
“Pretreatment can be undertaken if the raw water is highly contaminated and has debris, organic matter and suspended solids to prevent the filters from getting clogged,” Health Assistant Secretary Tagumpay Maniquis said.
He explained that a filter’s ability to remove contaminants depends on its size, noting that filters with a 0.1-micron capacity cannot remove contaminants smaller than that measurement.
“To deactivate viruses or bacteria less than 0.1 micron, you can boil the water or use a disinfectant. What is commonly used for disinfection is a chlorine tablet,” Maniquis said.
The DOH advised the public to coordinate with their local health offices on the proper use of chlorine tablets.
For those using water filtration systems to improve drinking water quality, the agency also reminded the public to check whether their devices are registered with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
“It should have undergone registration and been issued a certificate of health-related device registration,” Maniquis said.
The registration status of water filters and other treatment devices can be verified through the FDA’s online portal at https://verification.fda.gov.ph.
School gardens
In the education sector, Education Secretary Sonny Angara has directed schools to strengthen the planting of drought-tolerant and short-cycle crops to ensure the uninterrupted implementation of the government’s feeding program despite the threat of El Niño.
“We must be prepared and resourceful in the face of the challenges brought by El Niño. Under the administration of President Marcos, it is our priority to ensure that nutritional support for our students remains uninterrupted,” Angara said.
He stressed that protecting school gardens is essential to the government’s efforts to strengthen food security, mitigate hunger and promote child welfare.
Angara directed schools to adjust their crop selection and soil management systems to address prolonged dry spells, extreme heat and water shortages that could disrupt conventional planting cycles.
He recommended fast-growing, drought-resistant and nutrient-rich crops such as munggo, okra, malunggay, saluyot, alugbati and kamote.
Schools were also instructed to adopt water-saving measures, including organic mulching, rainwater harvesting, alternate-day watering schedules and drip irrigation.
For urban and space-constrained schools, the Department of Education will issue standardized guidelines for non-soil and vertical farming systems, including container gardening, hydroponics and stacked planting.
“This is more than just planting vegetables; we are teaching our youth about resilience and cooperation, while ensuring that there is sufficient, nutritious food on every table in our schools,” Angara said.
“With the help of our teachers, parents and local governments, we are strengthening our gardens to serve as a guide and a source of support during times of drought. Together, we are fostering the future of our youth,” he added.
Price control
Meanwhile, Sen. Francis Pangilinan has called on the government to strictly enforce price freezes and jail major hoarders who may exploit the impending El Niño crisis, warning of its potential impact on food production and consumer prices.

title: PNP monitors transport hubs
content:
PNP monitors transport hubs
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is maintaining heightened operational readiness and road safety across major transport hubs and primary highways as millions of Filipinos return to urban centers after All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. directed all police regional offices to sustain foot and mobile patrols, man assist desks and monitor high-density choke points to deter opportunistic criminals and prevent vehicular accidents.
Nartatez noted that the extended security drive aligns with the directives of President Marcos and Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla to safeguard the traveling public, prevent crime and manage traffic flow.
“As travelers make their way back to their homes, schools and workplaces, the PNP remains fully mobilized to keep roads secure, maintain public order and respond swiftly to any incident that may disrupt travel,” Nartatez said. “Our priority is to ensure that every Filipino reaches their destination safely.”
Under the directive, police presence will remain concentrated in bus terminals, commercial seaports, airports, train stations and transport interchanges.
The instruction comes after massive crowds observed Undas, with data showing that over 1.16 million visitors gathered in Manila’s two largest public cemeteries alone on Nov. 1, alongside millions more who paid respects to deceased loved ones in provincial cemeteries nationwide.
Nartatez urged long-distance drivers and private vehicle owners to adhere to traffic laws, avoid distracted driving and practice rest stops to prevent fatigue-related road crashes.
“No destination is worth risking lives for,” Nartatez stressed. “We urge motorists to follow traffic laws, avoid speeding, never drive under the influence of alcohol, refrain from using mobile phones while driving and take adequate rest before long trips.”
“As we conclude this meaningful observance, let us carry home not only cherished memories of our loved ones but also a renewed commitment to protect one another through responsible and law-abiding behavior,” he said.
Fewer bus travelers
The Philippine Bus Operators Association of the Philippines (PBOAP) has reported fewer bus travelers during Undas compared to last year.
“There weren’t that many queues in bus terminals. It’s also observable that there are less travelers now,” PBOAP executive director Alex Yague said.
Yague said passengers may have taken advantage of the long weekend to spread out their trips over several days, allowing passenger traffic to be distributed over four to five days and ease the usual surge of travel demand during Undas.
PBOAP noted that another factor in the fewer bus travelers is the increase in private vehicles traveling to provinces.
“Maybe because the fares and tolls have been expensive. Friends and other passengers may have done carpooling, while others might have their pasalubong delivered to their loved ones in the province,” Yague said.
Despite the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board approving over a thousand special bus permits, Yague said passenger figures have not exhausted the travel demand this year.
PBOAP said Undas travel now had a lot of advantages, including good weather and road conditions for faster bus turnarounds.
No major accidents have been recorded over the weekend, Yague said.
Meanwhile, Transportation Secretary Vince Dizon has ordered the Metro Rail Transit Line 3 (MRT-3) to deploy additional trains to assist at least 6,000 more commuters back to the metro.
According to MRT-3, 19 trains were deployed yesterday in anticipation of the expected increase in passengers returning home after Undas.
From Oct. 29 to Nov. 2, the Philippine Red Cross attended to 8,721 patients — Andrew Ronquillo, Rhodina Villanueva

title: Bobo na, magnanakaw pa
content:
Bobo na, magnanakaw pa
Bobo na, magnanakaw pa. (“Stupid or incompetent and a thief as well”). I declared during my Bilyonaryo TV appearance Thursday, Oct. 29.
“Bobo na, magnanakaw pa” has gone viral – 3.7 million views at this writing, 1.6 million views on Bilyonaryo TV and 2.1 million in its affiliate Abante.
Super host Margaux Salcedo invited me as a resource person in her Business 360 daily show, a business and economic program monitored by businessmen.
“We take advantage of your legendary status and longevity in business journalism,” Margaux greeted me.
A journalist for 56 years, I covered nine Philippine presidents, including the three dynastic presidencies – Diosdado Macapagal to Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Cory Aquino to Benigno S. Aquino III and Ferdinand Marcos Sr. to Marcos Jr. With 56 years of uninterrupted journalism, I probably am the most senior journalist in the Philippines today.
Margaux interviewed me on two issues – the peso drop against the dollar and El Niño.
In 2022, I recalled, the peso depreciated by 10 percent (from 50.77 in 2021 to 56.12 per dollar). Yet the economy grew by 7.6 percent – the best in 46 years.
“A peso depreciation could be good,” I asserted, “for our 12 million OFWs or expats working abroad because right now they are doing $35 billion (remittances a year). With the rate decreasing from 60 to 65 (pesos per dollar), they are now earning on average additionally P175 billion. P175 billion that can fund/run a complete Cabinet department today, for a year.” Compare the $35 billion to a foreign direct investment (in a good year) of $9 billion.
“We are also a net importing economy, and a big factor in our inflation is attributed to the global headwinds, the Iran war, uncertainty with respect to,” Salcedo countered.
My reply: “60 percent of our problems now is the Iran war. Iran war increased the price of diesel by 77 percent. It’s only now that I have heard of diesel at P120 per liter. It used to be P10 per liter. Gasoline, in fact, used to be P1 per liter.”
Margaux asked me about the propriety of Bangko Sentral Governor Eli Remolona being called to Malacañang for a briefing. I said that under the Constitution (and the law), the BSP governor is supposed to report to the President on economic and financial developments. Remolona (the world’s highest paid central bank governor) “is experienced and an expert,” I said. “He has spent most of his professional life overseas.” Besides, BSP manages the Philippine financial system (P38 trillion in resources) which I said grew 12 percent, meaning “there is money spinning around despite GDP growing only 2.3 percent a year.”
The problem, I pointed out, “is money is being stolen. And being hidden.” “Our problem is not a shortage of money. We have plenty of money. Our savings rate is 25 percent. On a GDP of P39 trillion, “that’s more than P7 trillion – P7 trillion money hidden in suitcases, under pillows, under beds.” “The challenge is to stimulate investments,” I said. Addressing thieves in government, I pleaded, “please bring out the money.” That hidden money, I said, “is one reason why the peso is depreciating. It is being used to hoard and bring out dollars, because the crackdown has started (on the corrupt). Politicians are being put in jail. (Senators) Marcoleta, Jinggoy Estrada, (pastor Apolo) Quiboloy.”
Margaux inquired about the current political turmoil. I said “we have been in worst situations. During COVID (in 2020), the GDP went down by 9.5 percent (the deepest drop in a century), yet the following year (2021), the economy grew 5.7 percent. “The recovery was robust. This is a very strong economy. It is the 12th largest consumer market in the world, 115 million people with per capita income of $13,000 (ppp). That’s huge.”
“Will the economy follow this pattern of rebound?” Margaux queried.
“The Iran war will worsen,” I said, “because Trump has been beaten by Iran and he will exact revenge after the midterm elections. It will be his last hurrah. He will use up all his missiles on Iran.” In that event, “the outlook, at best, is uncertain over the next two years. Even if the Iran war were to end today, the problem with energy (shortages) would persist for two-three more years. The facilities to produce diesel are gone. LPG gone, oil refining facilities gone. It will take time and money to rebuild those facilities. While these facilities are out, we will have shortages.”
On El Niño-induced drought, I said “I am not at all worried. Habagat (the southwest monsoon) brought in heavy rains (volume was seven times NCR’s demand for water) and filled up aquifers, the forests and the roots of trees. “It’s a matter of harnessing that water. We have plenty of water. Two-thirds of our territory is water. Why are we so worried about water? Singapore does not have drinking water at all. Yet, it has done 7-8 percent GDP growth.”
“Singapore has enough reservoirs,” Margaux countered.
“The best reservoir that we must preserve is our brain reservoir,” I cut in, “Banong-bano tayo. We are becoming incompetent. Nabobobo tayo (We are becoming stupid). Kasi naman ang ating mga politicians, saksakan ng bobo (It’s because of the politicians. They really are stupid or incompetent). Saksakan ng bobo (Really stupid). Ang sarap patayin (What a thrill to kill them!). Bobo na magnanakaw pa (Already stupid and thieves as well).
“Yan ang problema talaga natin (That’s really the problem.). Bobo na magnanakaw pa (Already stupid and thieves as well). Ang hirap ng combination (That’s a difficult combination). Kasi hindi naiintindihan kung mali ang ginagawa niya eh (Because they don’t know what he’s doing is wrong). Tsaka, pag hinuhuli mo siya, sasabihin niya na inaapi mo siya, eh. Kasi nga bobo (“Also, when you arrest them, they think they are being oppressed. It’s because they are really stupid).
Bobo na, magnanakaw pa!

title: One strait, one tank, one drought
content:
One strait, one tank, one drought
Every Tuesday morning, a rider I will call Jun fills his tank before the sun is up. He does it on Tuesday because that is the day the new pump price takes effect, and he has learned to read Monday’s news the way a farmer reads the sky. This week the news says gasoline goes up again by two to three pesos a liter. Three pesos a liter, ten liters a day, 30 pesos gone before his first passenger. Multiply that by every jeepney, tricycle and fishing boat in the country, and you see how a war in the Middle East ends up in a lunchbox in Caloocan.
This has been the hardest year for fuel in living memory. In March, when the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, diesel climbed past P130 a liter and gasoline past P110. The President declared a national energy emergency. Since January, gasoline has risen by a net of about P68 a liter and diesel by about P65. Jeepney drivers have gone on strike at least four times. Government helped with a fuel discount for jeepneys and a tax cut on LPG and kerosene, but the minimum jeepney fare has gone up by only one peso twice. Fuel rose by 60 and fares rose by two. That gap is why drivers are angry, and they are right to be.
Here is the part that should bother all of us. The Philippines imports nearly all of its oil, and most of it passes through that one strait. In the nearly 30 years since we deregulated the oil industry, the government has never owned a single storage tank for a bad day. Our fuel inventory, about 53 days today, sits in private facilities and mostly belongs to private companies. In a real emergency, the state has very little of its own to release.
That is finally changing, and it deserves more credit than it is getting.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin has been doing the unglamorous work. Last week she told Reuters the Philippines is negotiating with Saudi Arabia, Russia, the United States, Japan and others to store oil here, and that the government will start building its first state-owned tank in Bataan next year, beginning with one million barrels and growing toward a 60-day reserve.
In the House, lawmakers have filed a bill to create a Philippine Strategic Petroleum Reserve so the stockpile is written into law and does not depend on who sits in the department. For once, the executive and Congress are pulling in the same direction.
It is late, but it is right, and the secretary should be given room to finish the job rather than be asked at every hearing why it was not done 20 years ago.
But a tank is only half the story. The other half is water.
Next year is an El Niño year, which means less rain, lower rivers and hazier skies. Secretary Garin has said our hydropower output could fall by as much as 60 percent in the first half of 2027 and solar by 20 percent. When the dams run low and the panels dim, the grid turns to diesel and bunker fuel to keep the lights on. So the same drought that empties our reservoirs will send us back to the oil market at exactly the moment it is most dangerous.
We saw a preview in 2024, when El Niño gave the Luzon grid 11 red alerts and 31 yellow alerts in one summer. In 2027 we may get the drought and the war at the same time.
A country that plans for one crisis at a time keeps getting surprised. A serious plan has four parts, and none of them requires a miracle.
First, pass the reserve law before the Bataan tank is filled. A stockpile that exists only in an executive program can be sold, borrowed against or quietly forgotten by the next administration. Put it in statute. Say how many days it must hold, who can release it and when.
Second, treat water like fuel. El Niño is a water crisis before it is an energy crisis. A dam that holds water through the dry months is a strategic reserve too, and deserves the same urgency we are finally giving to oil.
Third, buy from more than one place. Every barrel that does not have to pass through Hormuz is insurance.
Fourth, reduce how much we need. Filipino households have quietly become some of the world’s biggest buyers of solar panels because they are tired of paying some of the highest power rates in Asia.
I say this as someone whose company lives and dies by the price of gasoline. Every household that makes its own power is one less that waits on Monday’s news with dread.
None of this is cheap. A full reserve has been estimated at more than P150 billion, and critics will fairly ask whether that money should go to grids and renewables instead. I would fund both.
Every price spike is already a tax, collected by foreign producers and paid by Filipino commuters, with nothing left behind. A reserve, a dam, a charging network. These are taxes we pay to ourselves, and they stay.
Jun does not care whether the tank is in Bataan or Singapore. He cares whether, on a bad week in 2027, the pump price moves by one peso instead of 10. That is what a reserve buys. Not cheap fuel forever, but a buffer between a missile strike and a man’s dinner table.
We are finally building the reserve. Let us write it into law, and build the water reserve beside it, before the dry season reminds us why.
The best time to dig the well was before the drought. The second best time is now.

title: The myth of the ‘perfect victim’
content:
The myth of the ‘perfect victim’
In the month leading to International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, which we commemorate on Nov. 25, an allegation of sexual assault at a prestigious university has re-ignited discussion about the safety of women, the requirements of consent and the rape myths that create the idea of the “perfect victim.” The incident concerning the so-called “Cornell 7” reached international news upon the filing of a civil case by the alleged victim, who claimed that seven fraternity members allegedly drugged and sexually assaulted her over several hours in October 2024. The civil lawsuit, coupled with other reports as well as statements from Cornell – which had conducted its own investigation after the events, which is also currently under scrutiny – allows a timeline to be created that shows the nature of the circumstances as we know it surrounding the incident in October 2024:
The woman who filed the suit, referred to as Jane Doe, drank alcohol at her sorority house and at the bar where the fraternity party was taking place, where she was allegedly served alcohol despite saying she was underage. Later that night she arrived at the fraternity house “visibly intoxicated” and says that she was pressured into taking ketamine by two fraternity brothers who then propositioned a threesome. Afterwards, one of the men allegedly sends a message to the fraternity’s Snapchat group of more than 50 men, suggesting that she was available for “free” sex; another member later asked “Shop still open?” and received the response, “Yea.”
Multiple fraternity members allegedly show up and rape her over several hours, even “pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them,” before the woman loses consciousness. The woman sent some apparently friendly texts to members of the fraternity for a few days after, but that quickly changes and around two weeks later she reports the incident to the campus police, where she states that “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped” – but it is now known that the campus police omitted this in the report they sent to the prosecutor.
Cornell University commenced what is known as a Title IX investigation, holding multiple hearings over a four-week period, and eventually two of the accused were expelled, two suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct. Allegedly, at least some of the accused were directed to undergo training and “write reflective essays” and none of the accused are criminally prosecuted. However, Jane Doe was not informed of the results of the investigation. She filed her civil lawsuit in September this year.
The allegations made by Jane Doe and the failure of institutional action that followed is horrific to me and to many others, and yet while much of the reaction to the case was of condemnation and calls for action, the circumstances attendant to the event and all that surrounded it provided, unfortunately, fertile ground for victim blaming and a regurgitation of myths and misconceptions about rape and consent.
Those who would excuse the assault point to Jane Doe’s initial willing consumption of alcohol as somehow disqualifying her claim to have been mentally incapacitated by drugs or drink – a position that has been codified into law in certain places, including New York where the alleged assault took place.
As happens all too frequently, there was also no shortage of people that went after the character of Jane Doe herself – the differing tenor of her accounts of what happened, or her choice to drink or attend the party in the first place, such as an opinion piece in USA Today which ended with the line: “Regretting one’s bad decisions is a far cry from rape.” The persistence and prevalence of these opinions – and the belief that something is not “real rape” unless it adheres to strict conditions, which include the pristine virtue of the victim – show how much work still has to be done to explain the concept of consent and the inherent and equal dignity of women.
A woman is not property, to be passed around or offered to others like a bag of chips. A woman’s refusal is not of less value than a man’s request, nor can it be presumed to encompass more than anything explicitly said. A woman’s right to her body is in no way lessened by what she wears, by whom she has chosen to sleep with in the past, by her looks, job, social class or disposition.
A helpful acronym that has been used to understand the nature of consents is that of F-R-I-E-S. Consent must be:
• Freely given; not a product of deception, intoxication, coercion or pressure;
• Reversible at any time; a yes only lasts until it becomes a no, there is no such thing as “touch move;”
• Informed; it must be given with full knowledge of what is being agreed to, and what was agreed to cannot be changed without consent being required anew;
• Enthusiastic; uncertainty is not consent, nor is acquiescence because of expectation or peer pressure – it must come from a genuine desire to say yes.
• Specific; there is no room for hidden meanings – a yes to a date is not a yes to sex, a yes to sex is not a yes to film it.
What makes the Cornell 7 case resonate with so many is not because it is rare, it is because that such treatment of women and the manner by which these acts are defended is all too common, and a sign of the underlying misogyny that must be rooted out.
The attitude that allows men in private groups to talk about women like property is the same that leads to men trafficking Filipino women as “mail-order-brides,” then forcing them to work as prostitutes. These attitudes are not harmless, or traditional, or something that can be excused by “boys will be boys.”
Boys, and girls, will be how we raise them to be. It is our job to raise them to understand consent, women’s equality and basic human dignity. Or else acts of violence against women will remain commonplace, and that is unacceptable.
Consent and sexual education must be a priority of our schools, and schools and workplaces both must have zero tolerance for cultures of misogyny.

title: Big Boy’s hot pitch: A nationwide solar/RE ‘power bank’
content:
Big Boy’s hot pitch: A nationwide solar/RE ‘power bank’
Don’t we all love a reliable and handy power bank, especially when our mobile phone is almost running on empty and we don’t have access to electricity just yet or, worse, when an outage suddenly hits?
Now imagine something like that but on a grand scale – a battery energy storage system (BESS) that could help power millions of households all over the country, especially now that we’re experiencing an energy crisis.
Tycoon Henry “Big Boy” Sy Jr. is pitching this as a fast, practical and doable solution to the country’s power woes: allowing the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines to put up a chain of BESS facilities nationwide which NGCP could tap when certain areas don’t have enough power supply.
Project Airbag
Big Boy, vice chairman of NGCP, remained in his trademark cool and calm demeanor, but could not conceal the urgency of the situation as he discussed his proposal during a rare media chat last week.
Actually, you’d know a situation is bleak, even desperate, and already taking a heavy toll on the economy when tycoons start speaking out and pitching their own solutions.
Big Boy wasted no time and went straight to his point – the power crisis and how to solve it.
He calls it Project Airbag, perhaps because we are in an emergency and his proposal can provide fast-response storage, which in turn would strengthen grid flexibility, resilience and energy access.
Under Project Airbag, NGCP would put up an initial pipeline of 1,850 megawatts of BESS capacity. Of this, 850 MW are already ongoing in six sites across the country and 1,000 MW for 12 sites still for assessment. In the next five years, this could reach 10,000 MW.
A battery storage stores available electricity and releases it when the system is under pressure. It gives NGCP an additional transmission-side tool to support the system during short-duration shortages.
Putting up BESS facilities is faster than new generation can be built – less than a year, Big Boy said, compared to a power plant which could take up to seven years, sometimes even longer, to build.
The project is intended to help address immediate system pressures, prepare the grid for tighter supply conditions associated with the 2027 El Niño and provide longer-term flexibility as the country’s generation mix continues to evolve.
Big Boy said the priority is the Visayas, which is currently experiencing blackouts because of tight supply conditions and simultaneous generator outages.
A wider grid for 2027 El Niño
The battery rollout, however, is not limited to the Visayas, Big Boy said.
El Niño, he said, poses a risk to the whole country as it creates a foreseeable risk of reduced hydroelectric output, particularly in areas where generation depends heavily on rainfall and reservoir levels. The risk is national, which supports the deployment of storage in other parts of the grid as well.
Batteries can then work during periods of reduced hydro output or other system stress conditions.
In all, Big Boy said, Project Airbag is a practical intervention that NGCP can pursue within its own sphere while longer-term supply solutions are still being developed.
It’s not supposed to be a threat to generation companies because batteries do not create electricity and cannot substitute for adequate generation over prolonged periods.
The underlying structural requirement remains sufficient, dependable power generation.
The deployment is therefore intended as a proactive resilience measure rather than a reaction after supply conditions have already deteriorated.
Power producers react
During the chat, I told Big Boy that power generators may not like his idea.
True enough, the Philippine Independent Power Producers Association Inc. (PIPPA) immediately raised concerns on the proposal.
PIPPA said its concern is primarily who owns these batteries and how their cost is recovered, not with the purpose of the BESS itself.
“By the description alone, supplying energy during shortages and peaks and providing fast-response reserve support are the services that generation companies and BESS operators already offer competitively in the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market and under power supply agreements and ancillary services procurement agreements.
“PIPPA respectfully submits that NGCP ownership of such facilities, with their cost recovered through regulated transmission rates, runs contrary to the structure and intent of Republic Act 9136, the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, and to the DOE’s policy on energy storage systems,” PIPPA said in a position paper.
Reacting to this, Big Boy said laws were intended to help the people.
The NGCP, in a separate briefing paper on Project Airbag, likewise said that new generation projects take significantly longer to develop, finance, approve, construct and commission.
Airbag can provide a bridge during that development period by reducing immediate system vulnerability.
It’s really short-term transmission relief supporting – not replacing – long-term generation investment.
In a way, Big Boy said, it’s about democratizing access to energy, given that the current supply challenge is acute and pervasive.
Additional supply, he said, must therefore come from as many viable sources as possible.
The objective is not to concentrate or monopolize participation in the energy sector but to disperse the burden of addressing the country’s supply requirements by enabling more participants and resources to contribute, NGCP said.
“We really have to do something before it’s too late,” he said.
Will electricity prices go down? Big Boy is confident that it will.
And for that alone, it’s worth a try.

title: Symbiosis
content:
Symbiosis
After all the country suffered in the wake of the flood control scandal, the congressmen are at it again. Funds from regular public services were again shifted to pet projects distributed according to congressional districts.
The Supreme Court boldly ruled unconstitutional the practice of pushing regular expenditures to the “unprogrammed” category, thereby ensuring funding for pet projects. Undeterred, the congressmen repeated the scheme that had the effect of inflating the budget total.
It is not that our legislators learned nothing from the monumental infra scandal that continues taking a deadly toll on our economy. It is that they need to skim from the budget to survive the coming election year.
Three decades ago, Jose Almonte, then national security adviser to former president Fidel Ramos, aptly described our politics. He said we have a “pork barrel state” and this is the root of all the evil that traumatizes us.
We have a weak political party system for a reason. Political allegiance is not built on shared adherence to a program of government or a vision of the country’s future. Political support is mustered through transactional politics. Which is to say money politics.
Without effectively functioning political parties, elections are won on the basis of sheer name-recall in a contest were all contenders promise a bottomless cornucopia of state- sponsored social goods. Reliance on name-recall opens the way to celebrity politics. The political economy for this is fairly straightforward: the better known the candidate, the less campaign resources are necessary to build recall.
Our weak political party system is, therefore, a measure of the vitality of transactional politics. Voters are loyal to a candidate, not any party program.
Once elected, the winning candidate is expected to deliver patronage goodies to his voters. This is the popular notion of “public service.” It is not to build the nation. It is to distribute the subsidies.
Transactional politics is expensive. Constituencies expect to be pampered in between elections. Voters expect to be courted by the politicians. They expect elected officials to broker the delivery of services in their favor. This is why politicians are involved by way of guarantee letters for patients even if we have, in principle, universal health care. Elected officials are supposed to have financial aid ready for everyone in need.
Trapped in transactional politics, governments tend to spend way more than they earn. A pork barrel state cannot be fiscally prudent. Because of the nature of our politics, the Philippine government is driven into unsustainable debt.
We have seen the recent riots in France. With an outstanding debt that is bigger than its economy, the French government has lost the fiscal headroom to fulfill its end of the presumed social contract. With an aging population, government finds it more politic to spend for pensioners than invest in education. Thus the riots among the young.
This is an explosive situation. It repeats itself in many other countries where distinct constituencies compete for a larger share of the public spending pie. Whether in Kathmandu, in Jakarta or in Paris, the increasingly difficult economic conditions will make the young feel disenfranchised.
In our own case, the budget debate has the potential to spark unrest.
The House of Representatives hijacked the budget. They took money out of foreign-assisted projects, education and health to make way for 7,000 petty district projects. This is, of course, an election-year budget.
But in hijacking funds for strategic infrastructure, such as the commuter rail system, the congressmen’s interest run against the interest of the section of the elite that depends on national constituencies. The executive branch wants funding for its legacy projects restored. The senators will want funding for health and education left intact. In a season of scarcity, a battle looms between those who need to keep their home constituencies happy and those who want the agencies of national government adequately funded.
We have been hearing a lot of brave talk from senators about purging the 2027 national budget of all the insertions made by the Lower House – including that fantastic infra fund set aside for the President’s son. We will see next week, when plenary deliberation happens at the Senate, if the senators find the courage to wipe away all the distortions in the House version of next year’s budget.
The pork barrel state will fight back. They will remind the ruling faction that the congressmen’s ability to deliver the votes depends so much on their getting their way with the budget allocations.
The camp of Marcos Jr. might not be ready to wage a budget war against the congressmen. These district-level politicians, after all, effectively constitute the electoral machinery of a presidency whose public approval ratings are now under water. Without the support of the congressmen, Marcos Jr. has nothing. His electoral endorsement is, as things stand, a kiss of death.
But congressional support is contingent on the district-politicians getting their share of the gravy train. They need money to indulge in money politics.
Thirty-five of our most influential business associations have put out a statement demanding that the congressional insertions be stripped out. This is unprecedented. Over the next few days, spokesmen for civil society groups will flood media channels with horror stories about the congressional budget insertions. They will hold vigil over the budget hearings and the bicameral conference committee.
But money politics involves a deleterious symbiosis.

title: EDITORIAL – Dearly departed pets
content:
EDITORIAL – Dearly departed pets
As Filipinos remembered their deceased loved ones during Undas, public attention was drawn to a case involving another group of dearly departed: pets.
The city government of Bacoor in Cavite has ordered the closure of Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in the city following the discovery of sacks containing 29 dead dogs and cats that were dumped on Oct. 29 in a vacant lot in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
Some of the sacks contained the pets’ names, weights and identification tags. This led to their owners and to the crematorium.
Yesterday, the National Bureau of Investigation said it would conduct a probe of Ahjay Paws for possible cases of estafa and environmental violations. As recommended by the Philippine Animal Welfare Society, the NBI is also coordinating with the police and other agencies for the inspection of similar facilities.
Pet cremation along with funerals have been gaining popularity as fur parents treat their pets like members of the family deserving of dignified treatment in death. The fur parents also want to keep the ashes of their pets in remembrance.
The services can range from P3,000 to P10,500 depending on the size of the pet and the type of package. Some companies offer coffins for viewing before cremation or aquamation, which is water-based cremation. An urn is provided, and clay or ink paw prints and the pet’s fur samples may be kept in jewelry or glass domes as keepsake.
Fur parents who believe their pets are worth that kind of attention and expense upon death deserve to get the respect accorded to their dearly departed.
If those offering pet cremation services do not understand this, they should close shop. And if they cannot understand humans’ love for their pets, they should be able to clearly understand what it means when a merchant fails to deliver the service paid for by a client.
The owner of Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium may never understand the bond between humans and their pets, but he must know the meaning of estafa.

title: Debt payments ease to P1.65 trillion in 9 months
content:
Debt payments ease to P1.65 trillion in 9 months
MANILA, Philippines — The country’s debt service bill fell by 11.7 percent to P1.65 trillion in the nine-month period ending September from last year’s P1.87 trillion, reflecting the timing of debt payments rather than the easing of the government’s debt pile.
Data from the Bureau of the Treasury showed that the amortization payments likewise dropped by 27 percent to P878.21 billion in the January-to-September period from P1.2 trillion in the same period a year ago.
Roughly 84 percent of the total amortization or P741.01 billion was remitted to domestic sources while the remaining P137.2 billion were paid to external creditors.
On the other hand, interest payments increased by 16 percent to P772.05 billion during the nine-month period from P665.85 billion the year prior.
About 76 percent of the interest payments or P584.74 billion were paid to domestic creditors.
Broken down, the government paid P404.52 billion in fixed-rate Treasury bonds, P131.24 billion in retail T-bonds and P41.15 billion in Treasury bills (T-bills).
It also settled P187.32 billion in interest owed to foreign financiers for the period ending September.
For September alone, the debt service bill stood at P207.46 billion, down by 36.7 percent from P327.89 billion in the same month in 2025.
As of September, the current debt payments represented 80.7 percent of the P2.05 trillion program this year, as indicated in the latest Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing document.
Principal amortization payments had reached 83.7 percent of the P1.05-trillion full-year allocation, while interest payments made up 77.5 percent of the P995.61-billion program.
Latest data showed that the Philippines’ outstanding debt climbed to a record P19.66 trillion as of end-September, due to additional borrowings and peso depreciation.

title: Sunlight Air delays jet acquisition plan
content:
Sunlight Air delays jet acquisition plan
MANILA, Philippines — The boutique airline of millennial CEO Ryna Brito-Garcia has deferred its plan to buy a maiden jetliner, as it shifts from expansion stance to survival mode because of cost spikes.
On the sidelines of a Management Association of the Philippines forum, Brito-Garcia confirmed that her airline Sunlight Air is no longer planning to buy a single-aisle jet.
Brito-Garcia said several factors have played into the deferral, but largely due to the uncertainty on when jet fuel prices would come down.
Sunlight Air also reduced flight volumes on certain routes, including Coron and Siargao, to cut fuel consumption.
The bigger concern for Sunlight is that travel demand is pulled by the double whammy of a weak peso and surging prices. Brito-Garcia said Filipinos tend to spend less on non-essential items like travel in times of economic slowdown.
Given this, Brito-Garcia said Sunlight anticipates no recovery in flight demand over the next two years, placing pressure on the carrier to cut costs to pull through.
Sunlight, a boutique carrier that mostly flies to island destinations, is recording a load factor of at least 75 percent, meaning three in four seats are booked every flight.
However, this has been maintained by cutting flight frequency to select destinations, as Sunlight focuses on high-return routes for now for cost efficiency.
To date, Sunlight manages a fleet of four turboprops: three ATR 72-500s and one 72-600. It uses these aircraft to fly to island destinations Boracay, Coron, Romblon and Siargao.
As an airline with an all-turboprop fleet, Sunlight was one of the carriers pushed out of the Ninoy Aquino International Airport because of the policy to only accommodate jetliners.
Sunlight flew 92,846 passengers in the first half, down by four percent from a year ago’s 96,728.

“Their engineers and faculty could independently assess road dimensions, pavement thickness and construction quality before contractors receive payment,” it added.

The DA said that the country needs about 131,000 kilometers of FMRs, with about 55,000 kilometers still to be built.
By the end of 2028, the government seeks to complete around 10,000 kilometers or 18 percent of the remaining requirement.
About 4,500 kilometers of the target will be funded by the government.
On the other hand, the remaining 5,500 kilometers, which are valued at P83.4 billion, will be implemented through public-private partnership.

title: Binance partner reviews impact of $6.3 billion crypto hack
content:
Binance partner reviews impact of $6.3 billion crypto hack
MANILA, Philippines — BlockShoals Technologies Inc., the Philippine partner of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, is assessing the possible impact of a $6.3-billion cyberattack on its local regulatory sandbox project as the global platform moves to replace stolen assets and restore withdrawals.
In a statement, Block-Shoals said it would coordinate with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to determine whether the security breach could affect its operations under the regulator’s Strategic Sandbox (StratBox) framework.
The StratBox allows financial technology firms to test innovative products and services in a controlled environment under SEC supervision, with safeguards intended to protect consumers and manage risks.
“As an approved participant in the SEC’s StratBox, BlockShoals remains focused on its own regulatory responsibilities, particularly the protection of users, operational security and compliance with applicable SEC requirements,” it said.
The statement followed a massive cyberattack on Binance on Oct. 30, when hackers compromised its hot wallets, or internet-connected digital wallets used to store and transfer cryptocurrencies.
Binance estimated that about $6.3 billion worth of digital assets were stolen, making it the largest reported cryptocurrency theft on record.
Initial investigations pointed to a compromised employee laptop that allowed unauthorized transactions.
Binance later said investigators uncovered additional security breaches, although there was no evidence that wallet private keys had been leaked.
In its latest update on Oct. 31, Binance said it had replenished 90 percent of the stolen assets, up from 80 percent previously.
The company has set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover the losses, drawing on corporate funds, insurance reserves and its Secure Asset Fund for Users, an emergency fund designed to protect customers during security incidents.
Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals while conducting security checks but said deposits remained operational. It was targeting a phased resumption of withdrawals on Nov. 1.
BlockShoals secured SEC approval in May to test its proposed crypto asset intermediary services under the StratBox framework.
Under its partnership with Binance, BlockShoals serves as the local intermediary responsible for regulatory compliance, while Binance provides technology infrastructure and operational support.
BlockShoals urged the public to rely on official Binance communications and remain vigilant against fraudulent messages or offers to recover stolen funds.

title: ‘Insurance demand slowing as high costs squeeze budget’
content:
‘Insurance demand slowing as high costs squeeze budget’
MANILA, Philippines — Rising cost of living is forcing more Filipinos to put off life insurance purchases, while some business owners are withdrawing money from their existing policies to fund operations, with demand expected to weaken further over the next six months, according to FWD Life Insurance Corp.
FWD Philippines president and CEO Soon Liang Lau said the insurer has observed slower demand among lower-income customers as households prioritize essential expenses amid persistent inflation and economic uncertainty.
During a recent media roundtable, Lau said the slowdown has also extended to small and medium-sized business owners, some of whom have tapped their insurance investments to cover higher operating expenses, particularly fuel costs.
The withdrawals became more noticeable in the second quarter as businesses struggled with higher diesel prices and other expenses needed to keep their operations running.
Lau said the company is advising affected policyholders to retain sufficient coverage even when they need to withdraw part of their funds, rather than surrender their insurance policies altogether.
He warned that weakness in the mass market could worsen over the next six months as more households struggle to set aside money for financial protection.
Despite these challenges, Lau said FWD continues to record growth, supported by relatively resilient middle-income and affluent customers, as well as its bancassurance partnership with Security Bank Corp.
Bancassurance refers to the sale of insurance products through banks, allowing insurers to reach customers through existing banking relationships.
The company’s agency distribution business has also remained stable despite weaker demand in certain market segments.
The slowdown in some customer segments comes even as the broader insurance industry continues to report higher premium collections.
According to the Insurance Commission (IC), life insurance premium collections rose by 17.9 percent to P229.98 billion in the first half from P195.05 billion a year earlier, largely driven by variable life insurance products.
Meanwhile, FWD maintained its position as the country’s largest life insurer in terms of new business annual premium equivalent (NBAPE) in the first half, recording P5.26 billion, 23.5 percent higher year-on-year.
The company captured a 12.2-percent market share, supported by its agency network, bancassurance operations and expanding product offerings.
FWD chairman and former Philippine central bank governor Jose Cuisia Jr. said the Philippine insurance industry still has considerable room to expand, although limited household purchasing power remains a major obstacle.
“What we lack is the purchasing power because our per capita income is still way below Thailand, Malaysia, not to mention Singapore,” Cuisia said.
He also pointed to the country’s wide income inequality, saying stronger growth in the middle-income population would help expand insurance ownership over the longer term.
Latest IC figures showed that insurance penetration stood at 1.96 percent in the second quarter, up from 1.8 percent a year earlier but below the 2.04 percent recorded in the previous quarter.
Amid changing customer preferences, FWD is expanding its traditional insurance offerings to complement variable universal life (VUL) policies, which combine life insurance protection with investments whose returns depend on market performance.
Looking ahead, Lau identified P10 billion in annual new business sales as an important milestone, while expressing ambitions to eventually expand the business toward P15 billion to P20 billion.
However, he did not provide a firm timetable or formal growth target for reaching those levels.
The company is also looking to strengthen its presence outside Metro Manila, particularly in Cebu, as it seeks to expand its distribution network in the Visayas and Mindanao.
Lau said building an agency network in provincial markets requires substantial investment, particularly in areas where established insurers already have a strong presence.
He also expressed hopes of making FWD’s customer servicing operations more artificial intelligence-enabled within the next six to 10 months to improve efficiency and customer experience.

title: ERC wants longer-term power reserve deals
content:
ERC wants longer-term power reserve deals
MANILA, Philippines — The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) is pushing for longer-term ancillary service procurement agreements (ASPAs) to limit the grid operator’s exposure to the Reserve Market.
ERC chairman and CEO Francis Saturnino Juan said allowing the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP) to lock in contracts beyond five years would help shield consumers from price shocks.
“What we want is a market that will truly serve our consumers while at the same time encouraging participation and more investments by our generation companies,” Juan said in an interview.
Asked how long the contracts should run, he said they should have a “minimum of 10 years.”
As the sole buyer of reserves, the NGCP secures ancillary services or backup power to keep the grid stable during unexpected surges in electricity demand or sudden disruptions triggered by power plant outages.
These services can be procured through ASPAs or from the Reserve Market, where they are traded at spot prices.
ASPAs currently have a five-year term, after which the NGCP must hold another competitive selection process (CSP) to secure new bilateral contracts with power producers.
Juan, however, said some power producers choose not to participate in the CSP if they expect to get better prices in the Reserve Market.
Reserve Market operations remain suspended following an ERC review that found persistently high ancillary service prices, particularly in the Visayas and Mindanao.
In 2025, Reserve Market costs far exceeded those under ASPAs, putting additional upward pressure on electricity bills nationwide.
ERC data showed that Reserve Market prices added as much as P1.29 per kilowatt-hour to power bills last year, compared with a maximum of just P0.13 per kWh under ASPAs.
Ancillary service charges account for the bulk of the transmission costs passed on to consumers. The NGCP does not earn from these costs, as they are remitted to generation firms providing power reserves to the grid.
According to Juan, longer-term ASPAs would also help power producers secure financing for their projects and recover their investments over time.
“I’m a firm believer of markets, but these markets must be well designed so that they can operate in a transparent manner,” he said.
Following the suspension of the Reserve Market, the ERC has started consulting industry stakeholders to identify ways to improve the market. It is now preparing a formal proposal for submission to the Department of Energy.
The DOE had earlier blamed NGCP’s delays in securing ASPAs for the yellow and red alerts in the Visayas, which caused rotational brownouts.
The NGCP, however, argued that reduced generating capacity triggered the grid alerts, emphasizing that ancillary services should not be treated as replacement power.

title: Phinma keeps optimism despite El Niño, foreign exchange concerns
content:
Phinma keeps optimism despite El Niño, foreign exchange concerns
MANILA, Philippines — Phinma Corp., the diversified conglomerate of the Del Rosario Group, is keeping its optimism heading into next year despite concerns over the potential impact of El Niño and fluctuations in foreign exchange rates.
Phinma, a holding company with investments in the education, construction materials, property development, hospitality and community housing sectors, delivered strong first half results amid a weaker economic environment.
“We already saw the softening of the economy late last year, even before the war. So we already adjusted some of our systems. And then early this year when the war happened, we already adjusted,” Phinma president and COO Chito Salazar told The STAR.
“We’re kind of prepared for the rest of the year, regardless of what’s going to happen. I think we’ll do okay and our projections will remain as is,” he said.
Phinma’s consolidated net income rose to P363.35 million and attributable net income climbed to P20.11 million in the first semester, with revenues reaching P9.55 billion.
The performance was attributed to consistent growth in education, more efficient operations in the construction materials segment, the continuation of regional development projects in properties and community housing as well as stable domestic demand in hospitality.
However, Salazar said next year is troublesome because of El Niño.
“So our people will be squeezed on both sides. The high costs are going to hit them locally because food prices will potentially go up because of El Niño. But then the imports will also push that side. So we’re a little bit worried about that,” he said.
Salazar said the group is also worried about the foreign exchange, with tensions in the Gulf region contributing to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates.
“But I think we will still remain optimistic. The pressure is a little bit on us to find efficiencies and productivity. I think we’re in good businesses where the demand is needed. We’re feeling more of a cost squeeze than demand problem,” he said.
Despite the uncertainties, Salazar said Phinma continues to keep an eye on potential acquisitions, especially in the education sector.
“Always. Never going to stop because the market is so huge that the people need education,” Salazar said.
“We’re still looking at Davao. We’re still looking for markets in NCR. We want to enter the low-income market in Cebu because our school right now is not low income. And we’re actually looking at Vietnam also,” he said.
Phinma Education acquired early this year Southeastern College — its 12th institution in the Philippines and 14th in Southeast Asia — to further expand access to affordable quality education for underserved first-generation college students.
Even without acquisitions, Salazar said Phinma would also continue expanding its network of schools in the country.

title: Malampaya marks 25 years of Goal Zero safety campaign
content:
Malampaya marks 25 years of Goal Zero safety campaign
MANILA, Philippines — The Malampaya Onshore Gas Plant (OGP) in Tabangao, Batangas City has marked 25 years without a recordable safety incident involving harm to people or a significant process safety incident, underscoring its longstanding commitment to safe operations.
The plant has maintained its Goal Zero record since Sept. 28, 2001 through continuous operations, major maintenance campaigns, facility upgrades, and increasingly complex activities supporting the Malampaya Deep Water Gas-to-Power Project.
Goal Zero reflects Prime Energy’s commitment to protecting employees, contractors, visitors, communities, and the environment while preventing significant process safety incidents.
“Reaching 25 years of Goal Zero is a significant operational achievement, particularly for a facility that has supported continuous gas production, major maintenance activities, and increasingly complex operations over the years,” Prime Energy president and CEO Donnabel Kuizon Cruz said.
The record is sustained through strong safety leadership, open communication, and a shared commitment among employees and contractor partners. Regular safety huddles, safety observation cards, incident reviews, and an annual Safety Day reinforce a safety-first culture and proactive risk management.
This commitment was demonstrated during Malampaya’s scheduled maintenance shutdown earlier this year, covering both the shallow water platform in offshore Palawan and the OGP. The shutdown was completed on time with zero recorded incidents despite the scale and complexity of the work.
The milestone comes as Malampaya enters a new phase of development. Prime Energy is advancing the Malampaya Phase 4 project, which will develop additional indigenous gas resources, with first gas targeted by the fourth quarter of 2026 to strengthen domestic supply and extend the field’s productive life.
Malampaya has supplied indigenous natural gas to power generation facilities in Batangas since 2001, making it a key contributor to the country’s energy security.
“As we advance Malampaya Phase 4 and undertake increasingly complex activities, maintaining these standards becomes even more critical. Our priority is to deliver the next phase of Malampaya safely, reliably, and with the same operational discipline that has sustained the project for 25 years,” Cruz said.
Malampaya is a government project under the Department of Energy. Prime Energy and its joint venture partners (Prime Oil and Gas, Inc., UC38 LLC and PNOC Exploration Corp.) operate the Malampaya project under Service Contract 38.

Philippines banks keep profit streak in 9 months
Net income up 4.2% to P315.5 billion
MANILA, Philippines — Philippine banks’ combined net income increased by 4.2 percent to P315.47 billion from January to September, as stronger interest earnings were partly offset by foreign exchange losses and higher provisions for potential bad loans.
Latest data from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) showed that industry profits rose from P302.62 billion in the same period last year, an increase of P12.85 billion.
The industry’s total operating income grew by 10.2 percent to P1.16 trillion from P1.05 trillion, supported mainly by higher earnings from lending and other interest-bearing assets.
Net interest income, or the difference between interest earned on loans and investments and interest paid on deposits and borrowings, also climbed by 13.5 percent to P979.09 billion from P862.44 billion.
Interest income expanded by 9.8 percent to P1.34 trillion, while interest expenses edged up by just 0.7 percent to P356.35 billion.
However, non-interest income, which includes service fees, trading gains and other revenue sources, declined by five percent to P178.09 billion from P187.39 billion.
The decline came as banks recorded P35.87 billion in foreign exchange losses, reversing the P9.06 billion in gains reported a year earlier.
This partly offset improvements in other income streams, with fees and commissions income rising by seven percent to P144.30 billion and trading income jumping to P31.43 billion.
On the cost side, non-interest expenses increased by 9.8 percent to P638.46 billion, reflecting higher personnel and administrative expenses.
Banks also provisioned P168.69 billion for credit losses on loans and other financial assets, a 24.8-percent jump from P135.16 billion a year ago. These are charges recognized to account for loans and other exposures that may not be fully repaid.
Meanwhile, the banking industry’s total assets reached P31.6 trillion as of end-September, 9.8 percent higher than the P28.78 trillion a year earlier.
Total assets represent the loans, investments, cash and other resources held by banks.
The industry’s gross loan portfolio expanded by 11.4 percent to P18.13 trillion, while deposit liabilities rose by 7.5 percent to P22.64 trillion, reflecting continued growth in banking activity despite the slower increase in profits.

title: For young Pinoys, financial planning no longer about wealth building

For young Pinoys, financial planning no longer about wealth building
MANILA, Philippines — PhilPlans, the pre-need arm of the Philippines First Insurance Group, has identified a significant shift on how the younger generation views long-term financial planning as no longer just about wealth building, but also about emotional resilience and ability to manage life’s challenges.
Based on its PhilLife Meter: Feeling the Insurance Pulse of Pinoy Gen Y and Z study, PhilPlans said while traditional retirement is often seen as a far-off concept, 65 percent of respondents specifically seek peace of mind from their protection plans, while 64 percent demand financial stability as a non-negotiable benefit.
Perhaps most telling is the shift toward self-reliance: 78 percent of young Filipinos now identify themselves as their top protection priority for the next three years.
“We are seeing a generation that is more self-aware and financially intentional,” PhilPlans president and CEO Monico Jacob said. “They are not only seeking protection from risk but also looking for structures that help them stay financially steady through life’s transitions – from career changes and family responsibilities to retirement.”
Responding to this shift, PhilPlans has strengthened its suite of pension offerings designed to align with the evolving priorities of younger Filipinos. Among these is PhilPlans Futura, a plan that provides yearly cash benefit from the 10th to the 24th year, followed by a return of payment in the 25th year, allowing planholders to enjoy both consistent income and a substantial retirement fund.
There’s also Ingat Yaman Kaban which offers a more foundational approach to saving, delivering steady yearly cash benefits and a guaranteed lump sum by the 15th year – making it suitable for those building financial discipline while securing future liquidity.
These plan offerings are designed to be simple yet flexible, making them suitable for first-time planners, freelancers, young entrepreneurs and corporate employees alike. PhilPlans made sure they have created straightforward, high-protection plans that eliminate the complexity often associated with retirement planning to help young professionals build disciplined savings habits.
“Our goal is to remove the intimidation factor from financial planning. By offering simple plans with robust protection, we enable Gen Y and Z to secure that peace of mind today, so they can focus on living their lives fully,” Jacob added. “We help them develop consistent saving and long-term financial discipline that allows them to take control of their retirement journey early.”

title: EastWest earnings drop 24% to P5 billion
content:
EastWest earnings drop 24% to P5 billion
MANILA, Philippines — East West Banking Corp. saw its net income fall by 24.2 percent to P5 billion in the first nine months of 2026, from P6.6 billion a year ago, as the lender booked higher provisions for potential credit losses amid a tougher economic environment.
The decline came despite double-digit revenue growth, reflecting the impact of heightened credit risks on the consumer-focused bank’s earnings.
Provisions for expected credit losses reached P15.9 billion during the nine-month period as EastWest responded to a more challenging and uncertain macroeconomic environment. Its non-performing loan coverage ratio stood at 90 percent.
“Our underlying businesses remain healthy, with strong revenue growth and improving operating efficiency allowing the bank to remain profitable,” EastWest CEO Jerry Ngo said.
“The current environment requires us to maintain discipline in managing risk while continuing to strengthen the franchise for the long term,” he added.
Net revenues climbed by 16.4 percent to P43.4 billion from P37.3 billion in the same period last year. Net interest income jumped by 22 percent to P36.2 billion from P29.7 billion.
Service charges, fees and commissions likewise increased by 10 percent to P5.8 billion.
Expenses grew at a slower pace than revenues, rising by 10 percent to P21 billion from P19.2 billion a year ago. This helped improve EastWest’s cost-to-income ratio to 48.4 percent from 51.4 percent.
Pre-provision operating profit, which measures earnings before setting aside funds for potential loan losses, expanded by 24 percent to P22.4 billion.
EastWest’s balance sheet also continued to grow, with total assets rising by 14 percent to P631.8 billion from P552.9 billion a year earlier.
Loans increased by 11 percent to P399.9 billion, while deposits climbed by 12 percent to P466.4 billion. Current account and savings account deposits accounted for 77 percent of the lender’s deposit base.
Meanwhile, assets under management at EastWest Priority surged by 35 percent to P145 billion as the bank continued to expand its wealth management business.
Capital buffers remained above regulatory minimums, although key ratios were lower than year-ago levels. EastWest’s capital adequacy ratio stood at 12.2 percent from 13.6 percent a year ago, while its common equity tier 1 ratio eased to 11.4 percent from 12.7 percent.
The bank is planning a P9-billion stock rights offering, which is expected to reinforce its capital base and provide additional room for future growth.
“Our priority is to navigate the current environment with financial and risk discipline without losing sight of the bank’s longer-term opportunities,” Ngo said.
“By maintaining a strong operating franchise while actively managing risks, we are positioning EastWest to weather near-term uncertainties while building the capabilities needed for sustainable growth,” he added.

Over 100 streamers going live on Bloomberry’s new product
MANILA, Philippines — An online gaming unit of Enrique Razon Jr.’s Bloomberry Resorts Corp. will add more than 100 streamers this fourth quarter to its new product that combines live betting and interaction.
Bloomberry unit OnlyFun.PH is onboarding over 100 streamers, mostly from video-on-demand platform VMX, to host live sessions on its newly launched service FollowBet.
OnlyFun.PH vice president for player engagement Suzy Polyanska said the company aims to ride on the emerging market for live interaction in the Philippines.
FollowBet rolls live gaming, online streaming and real-time engagement into a single platform. It will be hosted by some of VMX’s stars such as Angeli Khang and Robb Guinto.
FollowBet, which is the country’s first of its kind, allows Filipinos to watch VMX celebrities go live and play games. They can also engage with them during broadcast as they bet on games.
“FollowBet’s immediate growth focus is centered on creator-led content, with over 100 streamers slated to onboard this fourth quarter alone to scale interactive live sessions,” Polyanska said.
She confirmed that OnlyFun.PH would be introducing more titles to its platform, as it builds up its gaming catalogue to meet demand.
For FollowBet, players will be sharing the stakes with VMX celebrities they are following, so if the streamer wins, so do their viewers.
OnlyFun.PH restricts access to its games to individuals aged 21 and above. Further, the company guarantees that every stream on FollowBet is guided by content guidelines.
Polyanska said OnlyFun.PH enforces a know-your-customer identity verification to authenticate each and every player’s credentials. FollowBet, as a product of OnlyFun.PH, also observes safety protocols to protect both gamers and streamers.
OnlyFun.PH, a unit of FUNaloMAX, is the digital gaming venture of Bloomberry, while VMX, owned by Viva Communications Inc., produces films with mature themes.
The online gaming industry is taking aggressive steps to capture more gamblers and keep them inside the platform, as competition tightens in countries where they are legally allowed.

title: 10,000 Kaizen ideas could make you broke if…
content:
10,000 Kaizen ideas could make you broke if…
What is the actual, monetary value of your employee suggestions? That question came to me when I read a recent post by my friend Darril Wilburn on LinkedIn. He claims to “have seen companies report a big Kaizen count while they were losing money.”
Darril, senior partner at Honsha. ORG and co-author of the 2026 book Courage, Humility, Kaizen: The Three Disciplines of Toyota Leadership says “a lot of organizations count how many Kaizen (ideas) they completed. Hiro (Yoshiki, his co-author) would rather ask, “how much time and effort are we investing in Kaizen, and what are (we) getting back?”
That’s a profoundly important question. In the corporate circus, managers would claim they are geniuses. They celebrate more than 10,000 implemented ideas on how to save paper clips and reduce production delays by three seconds and still wonder why their quarterly net loss remains staggering.
I messaged Darril to ask for more ideas. His reply: “Many organizations…report that number (employee ideas) as a sign of success, while the measure that says the business is losing money gets far less attention.”
That brings us to a question often raised by financially-oriented managers: “If we fix that bottleneck, how much measurable savings can we generate?” It’s not that simple. When a team saves two hours of searching for tools or spare parts across the shop floor, that time doesn’t automatically show up as savings on their income statement.
What you get is recovered capacity. Two hours of savings can be redirected toward producing more volume without overtime, doing more with the same headcount or solving other problems. That’s assuming management knows how to redeploy the recovered time.
Barriers to implementation
I have seen managers encouraging their people to give more ideas. The result is often a large number of suggestions submitted, but not their actual, vetted contribution to their profitability.
It’s like measuring a chef’s success story by how many recipe cards he has written while the restaurant’s financial statement remains in the red.
My latest client has calculated a significant, potential cost savings of P93 million (around $1.4 million) after one day of a Kaizen workshop participated in by 26 workers assigned in four groups.
I told them to consult with their accountants on the accurate figure. But even if they’re successful in getting only ten percent of that savings, they should repeat the process in other areas.
When I did a follow-up two or three months after the workshop, I discovered several issues preventing them from achieving success.
Instead, they talked about the following issues:
1. Lack of authority. They are not empowered to implement change brought about by their employees’ ideas. They support those ideas, but they often lack the authority or budget to implement them.
They hold titles like medieval warlords, yet they need three layers of C-suite approvals to buy a box of ballpoint pens or move the trash can three inches to the left of a work desk.
In solving this issue, I told their top management to set a clear threshold limit (like a $100 budget) where managers can immediately approve low-risk, low-cost ideas with zero health or safety implication.
Alternatively, empower team leaders, supervisors or managers to act as sponsors to defend a business case to decision-makers.
2. Management procrastination. When managers require their workers to submit ideas, but take too long to acknowledge them, the latter could experience feedback frustration. If this happens all the time, people would quickly realize that the suggestion box is simply a recycling bin.
Therefore, the solution is to implement a strict enforceable working day timelines like 48 hours for the acknowledgement. Then followed by a maximum five-to-ten-day schedule for evaluation and decision by a management committee, depending on the significance of potential savings and complexity of ideas.
In conclusion, don’t force employee ideas into a rigid, spreadsheet-driven financial forecast. Some improvements generate immediate savings; others identify capacity, improve safety, reduce frustration or prevent future losses.
All deserve attention, but their benefits should be measured appropriately within the culture of perpetuating small, daily improvements compounding so aggressively that waste never gets the chance to settle in.

title: USDA: Philippines to import more dairy products next year
content:
USDA: Philippines to import more dairy products next year
MANILA, Philippines — The country is seen importing more milk products in 2027 due to steadily growing demand, according to the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).
In a report, the USDA Foreign Agricultural Services said the Philippines is set to import 185,000 MT of skim-milk powder (SMP) next year, a two percent increase from the 181,000 MT forecast for 2026.
SMP is mainly used in food manufacturing and is one of the most imported dairy products. Products include sweetened condensed milk, ultra-high temperature liquid milk, ice cream and gelato and infant formula, among others.
It makes up about 40 percent of all dairy imports.
The USDA said higher input and transport costs, driven by rising fuel prices, tempered its import outlook.
“Due to a strong dollar against the peso so far in 2026, importation of SMP is expected to be tempered given rate fluctuation as this is a major food ingredient for food and beverage manufacturers in the Philippines,” it added.
On the other hand, USDA forecasts whole-milk powder (WMP) imports to remain relatively flat at 15,000 MT next year amid higher prices.
It noted that with higher prices, manufacturers may opt to import more SMP next year and keep WMP reserved for products that require nutritional properties.
WMP is primarily used among dairy processors and retailers for its rich, high-fat and calorie-dense content, which enhances flavor and texture.
The international agency also said the Philippines is forecast to import 171,000 metric tons of fluid or ready-to-drink (RTD) milk next year. This represents a three percent expansion from 166,000 MT.
The estimated growth in imports will be driven by increased consumption of fluid milk through the government’s milk feeding program and increased household use.
“The growth in imports is tempered by increased production of local fluid and RTD milk products, though the Philippines is still supplying less than two percent of their total dairy requirements,” the international agency said.
It noted that fluid milk production is expected to increase by 4.3 percent in 2027 to 48,000 MT, mainly caused by the expansion of dairy herds from both small-scale and large-scale producers.
The USDA noted that imports of cheese products are expected to increase by five percent to reach 63,000 MT due to growing demand for cheese in the country.
“We have tempered our forecast due to current transportation and logistical challenges, high cost of inputs including fuel and the currently active El Niño, which may have an impact on the production lines of supplying countries,” it added.
The agency places total cheese consumption at 64,000 MT in 2027, a five percent increase from 2026.
It noted that this was due to increasing consumer demand, especially among middle-to high-income urban consumers in the Philippines, who consume cheese on a regular basis, with 82 percent eating it at least once a week or more.
