title: DOE ready to defend new mining bid rules in court
content:
DOE ready to defend new mining bid rules in court
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Energy (DOE) is prepared to stand by its proposed framework for awarding mining and other natural resource contracts should it face legal challenges in court, its top official said.
This developed as an inter-agency mining council vowed to refine mining application rules as part of efforts to support better livelihoods, more accountable mining operations and stronger protection for host communities.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the DOE is carefully studying the legal implications of its joint administrative order (JAO) with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources before issuing the final framework.
“What we are just trying to do at the DOE is give everyone a fair chance and eventually maximize the benefits (of the contracts) to the country,” Garin said in a recent interview.
Under the proposed JAO, existing contract holders and operators must surrender covered assets to the government upon the expiration of their contracts.
Dubbed the national interest evaluation framework, the guidelines will also make financial offers the “sole ranking factor” among qualified bidders to ensure that the government receives the highest possible economic benefit from the auction process.
However, the proposed rules have recently drawn opposition from Japanese investors and local mining companies, which warn that the order could create regulatory uncertainty and undermine investor confidence.
Among the most vocal critics is the Consunji Group’s Semirara Mining and Power Corp. (SMPC), the current operator of the country’s largest coal mine on Semirara Island in Antique.
The proposed rules were introduced only after the DOE had launched its coal bidding round, contributing to delays that eventually led to the termination of the Semirara auction.
Garin acknowledged that SMPC and other prospective bidders interested in the Semirara coal mine were “not happy with us.”
But the framework would help ensure that most of the coal extracted from the mine would be used domestically, she emphasized.
“Because of the (Middle East) war, I would rather push for everything that we produce or extract within Philippine jurisdiction to be used here. We use imported coal from Indonesia. That does not help us, that kind of system,” Garin said.
The Philippines imports about 95 percent of its coal supply, with Indonesia as the major supplier. This heavy reliance on imports leaves the country vulnerable to price volatility, particularly during supply chain disruptions or changes in other countries’ export policies.
Garin warned that the Semirara coal auction could face further delays if the JAO is challenged and the court “tells us to stop.”
Meanwhile, the Mining Industry Coordinating Council (MICC) is looking to refine mining regulations to make it easier for small-scale miners to operate legally while ensuring better protection for communities hosting mining projects.
MICC chair and Finance Secretary Frederick Go, together with co-chair and Environment and Natural Resources Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna, agreed to pursue several policy changes during MICC’s 52nd and final meeting of the year on Oct. 27.
“The council agreed to refine mining application rules while maintaining safeguards, strengthen local government notification on consultation concerns, and include provisions to restore Indigenous Peoples’ control of ancestral lands after mining and rehabilitation obligations are met,” the Department of Finance (DOF) said in a statement.
It also said that the council pushed for faster clarification of tax exemptions for registered small-scale miners with interim contracts, helping them operate legally and sell gold through the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas.
Former president Rodrigo Duterte signed Republic Act 11256 in 2019, which exempts registered small-scale miners who sell gold to the central bank from paying income and excise taxes. — Aubrey Rose Inosante

title: SEC wants independent directors in firms with government contracts
content:
SEC wants independent directors in firms with government contracts
MANILA, Philippines — The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is preparing to enforce stricter governance on corporations vested with public interest or those with significant government contracts.
SEC commissioner Rogelio Quevedo said the commission would come out with a new definition of corporations vested with public interest. Those which will be classified as such will be required to elect independent directors.
He said corporations vested with public interest include contractors and those involved in flood control projects.
“We have noticed – I particularly, as the head of the governance department – that there are corporations whose capitalization is only P1 million, but were awarded with government contracts worth more than billions of pesos,” Quevedo said.
“So you can expect that in the coming months, the SEC will come up with a new definition of corporations vested with public interest, so that we will now be requiring the presence of independent directors in corporations vested with public interest,” he said.
Independent directors are described as persons who are independent of management and the controlling shareholder.
They must be free from any business or other relationship that could, or could reasonably be perceived to materially interfere with their exercise of independent judgment in carrying out their responsibilities as directors.
“As the supervising commissioner of governance, I am advocating that there must be independent directors not only in publicly listed companies, but also in corporations vested with public interest,” Quevedo said.
He said good governance goes beyond regulatory compliance, as it strengthens competitiveness, builds investor confidence and supports sustainable growth.
“The SEC is guaranteeing that it will safeguard good governance. Good governance will at least be the saving factor for encouraging investments in the Philippines,” Quevedo said.

title: Gatchalian nanawagan ng mas mahigpit na pananagutan sa mga pet service provider
content:
Gatchalian nanawagan ng mas mahigpit na pananagutan sa mga pet service provider
MANILA, Philippines — Nanawagan si Senador Win Gatchalian ng mas mahigpit na pananagutan para sa mga nagbibigay ng serbisyo sa mga alagang hayop matapos matagpuan ang 29 na patay na aso na nakasilid sa mga sako at iniwan sa San Jose del Monte, Bulacan.
Ayon kay Gatchalian, nakalulungkot ang pagkakadiskubre sa mga bangkay ng mga alagang hayop na itinapon sa ganitong paraan, na aniya’y malinaw na paglabag sa mga batas pangkalikasan at pangkalinisan.
“Mas masakit pa rito, nagbayad ang mga nagluluksa at nawalan ng alagang hayop para sa maayos na huling pamamaalam sa kanilang minamahal na mga kasama, ngunit itinapon lamang ang mga ito na parang basura sa gilid ng kalsada.
“Malinaw itong kaso ng panlilinlang at kailangang managot ang mga responsable sa naturang paglabag,” ani Gatchalian.
Dahil dito, hinikayat ng senador ang mga lokal na pamahalaan (LGUs) at mga kinauukulang ahensya, kabilang ang Bureau of Animal Industry (BAI), na magsagawa nang masusing inspeksyon at audit sa lahat ng pet service providers, lalo na sa mga crematorium para sa mga alagang hayop.
Aniya, dapat tiyakin na ang mga naturang negosyo ay may kaukulang mga lisensya, sumusunod sa mga pamantayan sa pangangalaga ng kalikasan, at may mataas na antas ng integridad upang maiwasang maulit ang insidente.
“Bilang isa ring pet parent, nakalulungkot at nakakabahala na makarinig ng ganitong pagtrato sa mga alaga nating itinuturing na mga miyembro ng pamilya,” dagdag ni Gatchalian.

title: House prosec handa sa cross exam kina VP Sara, Mans
content:
House prosec handa sa cross exam kina VP Sara, Mans
MANILA, Philippines — Nakahanda ang prosecution panel na isailalim sa cross-examination sina Vice President Sara Duterte at ang mister nitong si Atty. Manases “Mans” Carpio sakaling iharap sila ng defense panel bilang mga testigo sa pagpapatuloy ng Senate impeachment trial sa Nobyembre 9.
Ayon kay House lead prosecutor Gerville “Jinky” Luistro, posible umanong tumestigo ang mag-asawa upang magpaliwanag hinggil sa kanilang mga transaksiyong pinansyal at mga dokumentong iniharap ng prosekusyon kaugnay ng kasong “unexplained wealth.”
Sinabi ni Luistro na interesado ang prosekusyon na marinig mismo ang paliwanag nina Duterte at Carpio sa kanilang mga bank records, interes sa mga korporasyon at negosyo, at mga deklarasyong pinansyal.
“Interesadong-interesado kaming marinig ang kanilang testimonya sapagkat ito ang mga kasagutang matagal na nating hinihintay,” ani Luistro.
Bago ang sine die adjournment at Undas break, natapos na ng prosecution panel ang presentasyon ng mga ebidensya para sa Article II, kabilang ang testimonya ni forensic accounting expert Atty. Alexander Cabrera na nagsabing umabot sa P817.87 milyon ang paglobo ng kayamanan nina Duterte at Carpio, na maaari pang umabot sa P1.5 bilyon sa konserbatibong pagtataya.
Sa susunod na Linggo, ang defense team naman ni VP Sara ang maghahain ng kanilang mga ebidensya at testigo upang sagutin ang akusasyon ng umano’y “unexplained wealth.”

content:
PNP ikinakasa kaso vs pet crematorium
MANILA, Philippines — Ikinakasa na ng Philippine National Police-Bacoor City Police ang mga kasong kriminal laban sa pet crematorium na sangkot umano sa pagtatapon ng mga labi ng 25 aso at pusa sa San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan.
Ayon sa pulisya, kinakalap na ang mga ebidensya at dokumento upang maisampa ang kaukulang reklamo laban sa mga responsable sa insidente.
Natagpuan ang mga labi ng 26 aso at tatlong pusa na nakasilid sa mga plastic bag at itinapon sa gilid ng kalsada. Lumitaw sa imbestigasyon na ang mga may-ari ng mga hayop ay kumuha ng cremation services mula sa AhJhay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium sa Bacoor City.
Nagsimula ang imbestigasyon noong Oktubre 31 matapos magsumbong ang ilang pet owners. Nakikipag-ugnayan na rin ang pulisya sa mga lokal na pamahalaan at iba pang ahensya habang hinihikayat ang iba pang posibleng biktima na magsampa ng reklamo at magsumite ng ebidensya.
Sa isang pulong kasama ang mga pet owner, sinabi ng City Legal Office na nabigo ang crematorium na magpakita ng CCTV footage at mga dokumentong magpapatunay na naisagawa ang cremation. Napag-alaman din na hindi saklaw ng business permit nito ang animal cremation.
Samantala, hinimok ng Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) ang mga apektadong pet owners na magsampa ng kasong estafa laban sa crematorium dahil sa umano’y kabiguang maibigay nang maayos ang serbisyong kanilang binayaran. Kabilang sa mga natukoy na labi ang asong si Ivy, na muling ipina-cremate ng pamilya sa ibang establisimyento.

content:
1-2 bagyo, papasok sa PAR ngayong Nobyembre
MANILA, Philippines — Inaasahang may isa hanggang dalawang bagyo na papasok sa Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) ngayong Nobyembre.
Ayon sa PAGASA, ang mga bagyong pumapasok sa bansa tuwing Nobyembre ay karaniwang nagla-landfall sa Bicol Region, Eastern Visayas, o Caraga Region.
Tinataya rin ng PAGASA na maaaring dumaan ang mga bagyo ngayong buwan sa Visayas patungong Palawan o tumawid sa Gitnang Luzon. Gayunman, nananatili ang posibilidad na lumiko ang mga ito pabalik o tuluyang lumihis nang hindi tumatama sa kalupaan.
Sinabi rin ng PAGASA na makararanas ang malaking bahagi ng bansa ng mas mababa sa normal hanggang lubhang mas mababa sa normal na rami ng pag-ulan ngayong Nobyembre 2026. Maliban dito ang Davao City, Davao del Norte, at Agusan del Norte, kung saan inaasahan ang malapit sa normal na kondisyon ng ulan.
Mula naman Disyembre 2026 hanggang Enero 2027, inaasahang makakaranas ang buong bansa nang mas mababa sa normal hanggang lubhang mas mababa sa normal na pag-ulan.
Tinataya ng PAGASA na hanggang apat na bagyo ang maaaring pumasok sa PAR sa pagitan ng Disyembre 2026 at Enero 2027, habang dalawa o higit pa mula Enero hanggang Abril 2027.

title: What charges could those behind pet crematorium controversy face? Pangilinan explains
content:
Pet owners seeking justice over the alleged improper disposal of their deceased companions may pursue legal action against those responsible, Sen. Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan said.
In a statement on Monday, November 2, Pangilinan cited several provisions of Philippine law that could apply to the case involving nearly 30 pets allegedly dumped in a vacant lot in San Jose del Monte City, Bulacan, instead of being cremated as promised to their owners.
He said the alleged disposal of animal remains could violate Republic Act No. 9003, or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, as well as local ordinances on cleanliness and sanitation.
Meanwhile, those who allegedly collected payments from pet owners for cremation services that were not actually performed could face estafa charges under Article 315 of the Revised Penal Code.
Pangilinan also said those responsible could be held liable for damages under Article 1170 of the Civil Code for violating their contractual obligations.
“Kailangang mapanagot ang mga responsable batay sa ebidensiya at sa tamang proseso ng batas,” he said.
The controversy involves Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, which came under investigation following the discovery of the animal remains in San Jose del Monte and complaints from pet owners who paid for cremation services.
The establishment has since been shut down by the local government of Bacoor, according to Bacoor City Mayor Strike Revilla.
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has also launched a probe into the Bacoor-based establishment to determine whether pet owners were deceived and whether criminal charges may be filed.
READ: NBI launches probe on pet crematorium
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said the bureau would look into possible estafa charges under Article 315(2)(a) of the Revised Penal Code if evidence shows that payments were collected for services that were not actually rendered.
The NBI will also examine the facility’s business permits, equipment, closed-circuit television footage and records documenting the handling of animal remains. It has urged affected pet owners to submit receipts, cremation certificates and relevant communications to help build a case.
Pangilinan called on local governments and concerned authorities to investigate the incident and ensure that those responsible are held accountable. He also urged authorities to help affected pet owners file the appropriate complaints.
The senator recalled working with the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) during the 15th Congress to amend the Animal Welfare Act of 1998 through Republic Act No. 10631, which strengthened penalties for animal cruelty, neglect and abuse.
He also cited Senate Bill No. 2501, or the proposed Revised Animal Welfare Act, also known as Dolly’s Act, which seeks to establish an Animal Welfare Bureau tasked with setting and enforcing animal welfare standards.
These include providing animals with adequate food, water and shelter, access to veterinary services, and protection against cruelty.
Pangilinan said he would include facilities such as pet crematoriums in the final version of the proposed legislation.
“Ang pagmamahal at pag-aalaga sa ating mga alagang hayop ay hindi dapat matapos sa kanilang pagkamatay. Nararapat lamang na mabigyan din sila ng maayos at marangal na huling hantungan,” he said.
Meanwhile, PAWS said it is providing free legal assistance to affected pet owners and helping prepare the necessary criminal complaints against Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium.
PAWS is working with animal welfare group Luna and Furry Siblings, which is spearheading the investigation on the ground, to help pet owners seek accountability.
“Behind every pet’s remains is a grieving family who deserves answers, dignity, and justice,” PAWS said.
—Rosette Adel

title: European supermarkets hit by new fridge cyber attack
content:
- Delhaize stores hit by “IT incident” in Belgium and Luxembourg
- Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre says it is investigating local incidents
- Belgian SPAR stores, and Estonian supermarkets also affected
STOCKHOLM/BRUSSELS — Ahold Delhaize AD.AS and Colruyt COLR.BR said on Monday that an IT incident overnight hit fridges and freezers in dozens of stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish grocers ICA and Coop reported similar temperature spikes, with one store blaming a cyberattack.
The incidents follow an attack in France last month, in which police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing fires and food losses.
Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month after it detected suspicious activity in its infrastructure.
On Monday, the Delhaize supermarket chain realized there were temperature increases in the cooling systems, Delhaize spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. The company is investigating the incident.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Belgian refrigeration company Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s systems, told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyberattack, in which the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. Moelans’ office declined to comment when contacted by Reuters.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices once largely mechanical can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
Authorities have not indicated who could have been behind last month’s incidents. There were no claims of responsibility.
Swedish stores also affected
The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, told Reuters it was working on several incidents regarding refrigeration systems in grocery stores around Sweden.
One Swedish ICA store said on social media that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been “hacked” overnight and set to 50 degrees Celsius. It said later that the store had since opened.
At an ICA Baronen store in Stockholm, a notice said all the shop’s freezers were broken due to a cyberattack. The store’s sales manager said the attack happened at 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) and was noticed at 5.30 a.m..
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson at privately held ICA said in an email.
Privately held grocery retail group Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents. It did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“We have in recent weeks… identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” the cybersecurity centre’s Billow said.
An Estonian supermarket chain was also affected, with temperatures set to 50 degrees, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman CEO Jann Mutso told ERR. He declined to name the affected grocery chain.
—Reporting by Anna Ringstrom, Louise Rasmussen and Johan Ahlander in Stockholm; Inti Landauro in Brussels; editing by Terje Solsvik, Kirsten Donovan

title: Lawmakers urged to balance child online safety with digital rights as bills near reconciliation
content:
As Congress moves to reconcile two proposed measures imposing stricter safeguards on children’s access to online platforms, legal and industry stakeholders are calling for policies that protect minors from digital threats without unnecessarily restricting their privacy, freedom of expression and access to information.
The call took center stage at a policy dialogue organized by Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra and GoDigital Philippines on October 22, which brought together government representatives, industry leaders and legal professionals to examine the implications of the proposed SAFE Kids Act and SMART KIDS Act.
The discussions come after the Senate passed Senate Bill No. 2424, or the SMART KIDS Act, on third reading on October 8, followed by the House of Representatives’ approval of House Bill No. 11566, or the SAFE Kids Act, on October 12.
With differences between the two versions still to be resolved by a bicameral conference committee, the resulting legislation could significantly reshape how children access social media and other digital services in the Philippines.
The Senate version proposes prohibiting individuals below 18 from accessing social media and other high-risk digital services. Meanwhile, the House version sets a minimum age of 13, requiring parental consent and imposing feature restrictions on users aged 13 to 17.
The House measure also extends regulatory responsibilities beyond digital platforms and parents to include other industry players, such as app stores and operating system providers.
At the forum, titled “Safe Kids, Smart Policies: A Dialogue on Children’s Online Safety and Digital Rights,” Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra Chairman and Managing Partner Mark Gorriceta stressed the need for legislation that addresses online threats without imposing overly broad restrictions.
“Protecting children online is a responsibility we all share. But effective legislation requires careful consideration of how safeguards will work in practice, who will be responsible for implementing them, and how we can protect children without unnecessarily restricting freedom of expression, privacy, and access to information. The goal should be policies that are clear, proportionate, enforceable, and workable,” Gorriceta said.
Balancing protection with children’s digital participation
Renato “Aboy” Paraiso, executive director undersecretary of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC), highlighted the threats children face online, including cyberbullying, online sexual abuse and exploitation and online grooming.
He said stronger safeguards are necessary but cautioned against reducing the policy discussion to a simple question of whether children should be allowed to use social media.
“The question is not simply whether children should be allowed or prohibited from accessing social media. We must also consider how restrictions can be designed to provide real and measurable protection while recognizing children’s ever-changing capacities, their access to information, and their legitimate participation in digital spaces,” Paraiso said.
He also emphasized the responsibility of technology companies in addressing online risks, pointing to platform accountability and stronger safeguards as essential components of child protection.
Kankan Ramos, chief operating officer of marketing and communications agency InvictusPH, offered an industry and parental perspective, highlighting the role digital platforms play in children’s learning, creativity, self-expression and social connections.
Drawing from her experience as a mother and marketing professional, Ramos said technology has expanded opportunities for children even as it exposes them to risks that require attention.
“When I look at my daughter, I do not see a child whose world has been made smaller by technology. I see someone whose world, in many ways, has grown bigger because of technology. But I’m also her mother. I worry about what she encounters, who can reach her, and how online experiences might shape her confidence, choices, and well-being… Child protection is not optional…But neither is the children’s right to learn, express themselves, and access information,” she said.
She also called for greater transparency, data protection and responsible digital marketing practices, particularly as children increasingly encounter commercial content through creator videos, entertainment feeds and personalized recommendations.
“The policy question is not simply how many children can we keep off a platform. It is also what do we preserve for children while we reduce the risks,” Ramos said.
Privacy, enforcement and constitutional questions
More than age restrictions, the proposed measures raised questions about how platforms will establish users’ ages without compromising personal information.
Both bills envision age-assurance requirements and measures to restrict or remove accounts reasonably determined to belong to children covered by the restrictions. They also seek to address harmful content and introduce safeguards involving targeted advertising, profiling, interactions with unknown adults and features associated with compulsive use.
Foreign platforms would also be covered, with requirements to appoint local representatives and comply with directives from Philippine regulators.
However, age verification must be implemented consistently with the Republic Act No. 10173 or Data Privacy Act of 2012 and applicable National Privacy Commission rules, particularly the principles of proportionality and data minimization.
The extent of personal information collected, the entities responsible for processing it and the safeguards against misuse remain important considerations.
The proposed restrictions also raised constitutional questions involving freedom of expression, the right to information and parents’ authority to raise their children. While the state has a constitutional duty to protect the youth, restrictions must be proportionate to their objectives and should not go further than necessary.
Enforcement presents another challenge, particularly given the possibility of children circumventing age checks, shared devices within households and the capacity of regulators to monitor compliance.
The scope of exemptions will likewise matter. Certified educational platforms and digital news services are expected to be exempt, although the final coverage will depend on the reconciled legislation. How lawmakers define age-restricted platforms could also determine whether messaging and gaming services remain accessible to minors.
Lessons from other countries
The Philippine proposals come amid growing international efforts to regulate children’s access to digital platforms, although countries have adopted different approaches.
Australia, Malaysia and Indonesia have established a minimum age of 16, while the European Union has focused primarily on platform obligations, including risk assessments and age-appropriate design.
The Senate’s proposed under-18 threshold would be higher than those approaches, while the House measure adopts a tiered system that combines a lower minimum age with additional safeguards for teenagers.
India, meanwhile, treats individuals below 18 as children under its data protection framework rather than imposing a general social media ban. Its Digital Personal Data Protection Act requires verifiable parental consent and prohibits tracking or targeted advertising directed at children.
In September this year, India’s Supreme Court also asked the government to consider additional statutory safeguards for minors on social media.
Other developments illustrate the legal challenges surrounding age-based restrictions. France’s under-15 ban, passed in July, was struck down by the Constitutional Council in August. The council found the measure disproportionate to freedom of expression and privacy, citing its failure to distinguish services according to risk and inadequate safeguards for mandatory age verification. A revised bill is being prepared.
In the United States, more than a dozen states have enacted laws generally requiring age verification and parental consent for users below 16. Technology companies have challenged almost all of these measures, primarily on First Amendment grounds.
In a recent Ohio case, NetChoice, LLC v. Yost, a Court of Appeals panel voted 2-1 to uphold a law requiring parental consent before children below 16 can open accounts. The majority characterized parental consent as a limited burden addressing children’s entry into platform contracts without parental supervision.
These international experiences underscore the difficulty of designing restrictions that protect minors without unnecessarily cutting them off from legitimate digital services and support networks.
The Philippines is also a party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which recognizes that children’s rights extend to the digital environment. These include protection from harm, as well as rights to information, expression, privacy, education and play.
Six considerations for the final legislation
As the Senate and House versions undergo reconciliation, Gorriceta Africa Cauton & Saavedra identified six considerations for lawmakers: regulations should be risk-based and appropriate to children’s ages and evolving capacities; age-assurance mechanisms should protect privacy; the scope of regulation should be clearly defined; fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and access to information, should be safeguarded; obligations imposed on digital industry players should be proportionate and workable; and implementation periods should give stakeholders sufficient time to adjust.

title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump, lets California count all ballots
content:
AT A GLANCE
- The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's request to block California from counting mail-in ballots from over 20,000 registered voters alleged to be non-US citizens, allowing the state to proceed with its elections.
- California Governor Gavin Newsom welcomed the decision, asserting that it ensures a free and fair election, while the administration's claims of widespread noncitizen voting have been widely discredited.
- The case highlighted constitutional tensions between state and federal election administration, with a federal judge criticizing the administration's attempt to influence state election procedures on the eve of the midterms.
Acting on the eve of the US midterm elections, the Supreme Court quickly rejected on Monday, November 2, a bid by President Donald Trump‘s administration to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who federal officials allege are likely non-US citizens.
The justices denied the Justice Department’s emergency request just hours after it filed it, shutting down the administration’s claims over disputed ballots that could have affected thousands of voters and injected uncertainty into election outcomes.
The decision represented another defeat for Trump as his fellow Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterms. California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold.
The administration intensified its focus on alleged noncitizen voting in the run-up to the midterms. Multiple studies and state audits show that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.
The Supreme Court’s brief, one-sentence order on Monday did not offer any explanation of its action, as is common when it handles emergency matters. No justice publicly dissented from the decision. The court also did not ask California for a response to the administration’s request, a step that, when taken, usually signals serious consideration of an emergency case.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, called the decision “a welcome sight for all Americans given the disgusting and dangerous attacks on our democracy by the federal government.”
“Tomorrow (Tuesday), Californians can feel secure in knowing the state will carry out a free and fair election — just as we’ve always done,” Newsom added.
A federal appeals court refused the administration’s request on Friday.
The administration had demanded that California separate any allegedly unlawful ballots from other ballots and not count them until those voters are determined to be US citizens.
“Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” the Justice Department said in its request to the Supreme Court.
Trump has made false claims about widespread US voting fraud including in the 2020 election lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
“We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced,” acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a social media post after the administration’s filing earlier in the day.
Constitutional questions
The US Constitution assigns the responsibility of administering elections to states, though the federal government has some oversight. The lawsuit marked a rare federal intervention in the voting process and signaled a willingness by the administration to contest the election results in court.
The administration already sought to restrict voting by mail — a mode of casting ballots used more often by Democratic-leaning voters — but the Supreme Court in September rebuffed that effort. And a federal judge on Sunday dismissed the administration’s lawsuit concerning the US Senate race in Alaska.
The list of 20,000 registered voters was amassed by the US Department of Homeland Security and sent to California officials and to Los Angeles County officials.
The Justice Department sued in federal court on October 15, claiming California is unlawfully preventing its enforcement of a 1996 US law that makes it a criminal offense for noncitizens to vote in federal elections. The department said California’s action violated the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause, which holds that federal law generally preempts state law.
California has said that the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust and that the lawsuit threatens to deprive 20,000 people of their right to vote based on vague accusations. The administration’s process for scrutinizing voter lists to identify noncitizens is flawed and likely rife with errors, it said in court papers.
California has 52 seats in the House of Representatives, more than any other state. Democrats need a net gain of four House seats to win a majority in the chamber.
‘Bend to the will’
US District Judge David Carter in Los Angeles denied the administration’s request on October 28.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch,” Carter wrote.
Carter raised concerns over the reliability of the administration’s data, noting that people recently flagged by the federal government as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalized US citizens.
“If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Carter wrote.
The San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals also refused on Friday to block the ballots, emphasizing the state’s power over election procedures and California’s “comprehensive statutory scheme to ensure the integrity of its elections,” including a system for canceling registrations if a voter is shown to be ineligible. – Rappler.com

title: ICC wraps up pre-trial hearings as Duterte’s November 30 case nears
content:
AT A GLANCE
- The ICC Trial Chamber III concluded its status conference ahead of former President Rodrigo Duterte's trial for crimes against humanity, scheduled to start on November 30.
- Duterte waived his right to attend the last status conference, but will be expected to attend daily during the trial, which will include opening statements from the prosecution and victim representatives.
MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III wrapped up its status conference hearings on Monday, November 2, weeks before the start of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s trial for his crimes against humanity case.
A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial. This is to ensure that the schedule and other legal matters proceed smoothly during the actual trial days.
Duterte skipped his last status conference after waiving his right to appear. The chamber granted his request.
“Mr. [Peter] Haynes, we’ve agreed exceptionally because this is not likely to be a particularly lengthy status conference that Mr. Duterte need not attend this morning. But once the actual trial starts, we will expect, as we said, [his] attendance on a daily basis,” said Presiding Judge Joanna Korner.
The former president, who has been detained at The Hague, Netherlands since March 2025, appeared during his status conferences on September 16 and October 13, respectively. The September 16 schedule marked Duterte’s first-ever ICC appearance since his arrest in 2025.
During the Monday hearing, the parties said they will have opening statements when the trial starts on November 30. The prosecution will deliver a statement, followed by the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims or the lawyers of the victims.
Traditionally, the defense cannot deliver an opening statement, but Korner said the defense might want to give at least an outline of what Duterte’s defense will be.
“And I want to know if you’ve considered applying, not to open in full, but to give, if you like, the public and the court an outline of what your defense is going to be, along the lines of what happens in other jurisdictions?” Korner asked.
“We will certainly finalize that position within the next few days, and we’ll let you know for scheduling purposes. But I think it’s more likely than not that I will say something at the start of the case, given its stature, really, and the character of the accused and his status,” said Haynes, Duterte’s defense lawyer.
The prosecution said they will open their case and take about four to six hours, and around three hours for the victims.
Principal Counsel Office of Public Counsel for Victims Paolina Massidda said they asked the chamber if they can use Tagalog (Filipino) for parts of their opening statement.
“Our request is more, during the opening statement, we will make some remark in quoting parts of a narrative that victims provided to us, and we’d like to do that in Tagalog,” said Massidda.
“And the purpose is a lot of victims will be connecting to the hearing. For them, it’s also important to listen how we convey to the chamber what they narrated to us and their experiences, and they relate and connect much more if that is done in Tagalog,” she added.
But Korner reiterated that the Rome Statute or the treaty that created the ICC, provides for only English and French as the court’s working languages. Apart from saying that there are interpreters, Korner said Tagalog is not the language of all the victims.
“So while we understand that you want to relate to the victims, you want the victims to relate to what’s being said, all of it, everything you say, as I understand it…. will be translated in any event, interpreted,” the presiding judge explained.
Schedule, witnesses
For the first batch of evidence, Korner said the chamber will adopt a new schedule. Like what had been announced in the past, there will be 30-minute breaks per hour to heed the experts’ advice that no sitting for Duterte beyond one hour. The schedule of sessions is as follows:
- 10:00 – 11:00 am
- 11:00 – 11:30 am (break)
- 11:30 am to 12:30 pm
- 12:30 to 1:30 pm (lunch break)
- 1:30 – 2:30 pm
- 2:30 – 3:00 pm (break)
- 3:00 – 4:00 pm
For the hearings in 2027, the parties — prosecution, victims, and defense — proposed the following schedule:
- January 11 to 29 (three weeks)
- One-week break (Feb 1-5)
- February 8 to 19 (two weeks)
- Two-week break (Feb 22-March 5)
- March 8 to 26 (final three weeks)
“I think, from all of us, if it’s possible to have the week of the 22nd of February off, and that is because that is when it’s a school break for all the different schools, the Dutch, British, French, and so that affects many people, I think, on the different teams,” said the Prosecution’s senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls.
Meanwhile, the chamber said the prosecution will present five witnesses for the first batch of evidence. The first witness will take six hours, a “little much shorter” time for the other two, then four hours each for the last two witnesses.
Korner also asked the prosecution if it was possible to prioritize the in-person witnesses, before presenting witnesses who will testify via video link. Nicholls said they have at least 29 witnesses who will testify online.
Once again, the large data set of evidence against Duterte, a subject of debate in the last status conferences, was brought up.
Nicholls said they will discuss the matter to straighten things out.
“And so we’re planning on having meetings this week to see about ways we may be able to reach agreements, which, as we started talking about this, if we can come to some agreements, that may sort of extract the relevance of a lot of, or not relevance, but extract the need to rely on much of that if we can come to some agreements,” said the prosecution lawyer.
The court also went into private or closed sessions multiple times during the Monday hearing. The chamber does this when there are matters that are private or confidential in nature that need to be discussed. – Rappler.com

title: Filipino embalmers – last caretakers of the dead, seldom cared for
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Jonnel Cribello, a licensed embalmer and trainer, highlights the evolving perception of embalmers in the Philippines, transitioning from being viewed as uneducated and untidy to recognized professionals.
- The Department of Health has implemented regulations to professionalize embalming, including mandatory training, licensure exams, and minimum wage standards, although many embalmers still face low pay and lack representation in licensing bodies.
PART 1 | Inside the world of Filipino embalmers
Last of 2 parts
When Jonnel Cribello received his license to embalm in 2009, one question followed him everywhere.
“The most frequent question people asked me [was] whether I washed my hands before shaking theirs,” he said.
A registered nurse who once dreamed of becoming a surgeon, Cribello turned to embalming after coming across a media feature on an embalming school. “If I wanted to work with the human body, the easiest route for me then was to work in the mortuary industry,” he said.
Today, he helps teach the next generation of embalmers as an accredited trainer and program director at the Philippine College of Advanced Studies (PCAS) in Cebu, one of only four active accredited embalming schools in the country and the only one outside Luzon.
Embalmers disinfect, preserve, and restore a body so families can hold a wake — often for days — before burial or cremation.
But while the industry has made strides in shedding its perception as dirty work, the systems around it — licensing, data, and pay — have been slower to catch up with other medical-adjacent fields.
Changing image
For years, embalmers were seen as untidy and uneducated, said James Patrick Ovejera, president of the Professional Embalmers Association of the Philippines Inc. (PEAP).
“There was an idea that it’s dirty work, the person is untidy, the person is illiterate, and the person is technically a low-class person,” he said. “There were even depictions in the movies wherein it’s a person that works in a dark place… a hunchback.”
That image began to shift around 2010, when the Department of Health (DOH) set out to professionalize the field, Ovejera said.
The rules governing embalming date back to 1975, when then-president Ferdinand E. Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 856, or the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines. Its chapter XXI, on the disposal of dead persons, covers everything from burial grounds to funeral and embalming establishments.
Detailed rules for embalmers came only in 1996, more than two decades later. They called for the DOH to create a Committee of Examiners for Undertakers and Embalmers (DOH-CEUE), which licenses embalmers and accredits training schools.
In 2010, the DOH reinstated the committee with new members, who worked with the University of the Philippines to streamline the curriculum and licensure exam, under Administrative Order No. 2010-0033. The order also, for the first time, mandated minimum wage for all embalmers.
The committee and the five training schools at the time then went region by region to explain the rules to local officials. Feedback led to new measures, including a refresher program for embalmers with long-expired licenses and a Filipino version of the exam, which was previously in English.
“There are a lot of people [who] are very skilled coming from the provinces…but they couldn’t really understand English well,” said Ovejera. At the time, he had been teaching at the Philippine Embalmers and Undertakers Review and Training Center (PEURTC), and enlisted in the roadshow efforts.
In 2018, embalmers like Ovejera formed PEAP as their own professional counterpart to the Philippine Mortuary Association, which represents funeral homeowners.
“At the time, there was no collective body representing us, and we wanted to do something about that,” he said.
In the classroom
Under current DOH rules, aspiring embalmers need a high school diploma, at least 140 hours of instruction from an accredited institution, and proof that they have embalmed at least 10 cadavers within a year. They then take a licensure exam held twice a year, every March and September.
Under rules revised in 2021, licenses are issued by the DOH’s Health Facilities and Services Regulatory Bureau (HFSRB) after applicants pass the committee’s exam. These are valid for three years and can be revoked if not renewed within five.
Students spend about two months in class and a month embalming real cadavers at partner funeral homes. Tuition ranges from about P27,000 to about P30,000 depending on the training institution.
Over half of Cribello’s students at PCAS have worked in funeral homes or come from families that own one. His oldest student was 75; the average age is around 45.
“It’s such a unique challenge because people [are] going back to school after years of not having a good habit of reading or studying,” he said.
PCAS now runs two cohorts a year of about 60 students each, up from 10 per cohort in 2009. At PEURTC in Manila, where Ovejera still teaches, local classes run 40 to 60 students, plus a separate class of five to eight from neighboring Southeast Asian countries like Singapore, Thailand, and Malaysia who come to the Philippines for mortuary education. Affordability and English as a medium of instruction are the main attractions.
Tools of the trade
Philippine embalmers train on only a handful of tools and chemicals. In the US, Cribello estimated, training incorporates 30 to 35 pieces of equipment.
“There are very simple kinds and sets of tools that have been used in the past and continue to be taught today here. That much has not changed,” he said.
Most local funeral homes rely on formalin, a cheap formaldehyde solution. Other chemicals used abroad, in what is called soft embalming, can make a face look more natural.
But culture and climate shape the practice, Ovejera said. Filipino wakes routinely run around the clock for days, sometimes weeks, and softer chemicals do not hold up in humid weather.
Cost matters too. A 200-liter drum of formalin costs around P11,000 to P15,000, while soft-embalming chemicals can cost 20 times more, according to Ovejera. For that reason, only select funeral homes offer more technical and upscale embalming options.
An industry behind
Demand for an embalmer’s work is guaranteed. Fair pay, Cribello said, is not.
“There is a certain opportunity to review the industry regulations in terms of the kind of salaries imposed within the industry,” Cribello said. “I personally feel that we are behind [compared with] similar professionals like nurses and doctors.”
Entry-level salaries still hover around minimum wage (P401 to P755 per day, depending on the region), according to PCAS and PEAP, and embalmers get no hazard pay despite chronic exposure to chemicals like formaldehyde, which the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies as a Group 1 carcinogen.
The 2010 rules set minimum wage as the entry point, Ovejera said, but smaller funeral homes often pay per body instead, pushing many embalmers to freelance and work between funerary businesses.
Change in any regard would require legislation. “I agree that there must be changes. But how do we do that? It has to be in legislation,” Ovejera said.
Embalmers also have no seat on the body that licenses them. Under the current rules, the DOH-CEUE’s five members are a chairperson, vice chairperson, sanitary engineer, pathologist, and legal officer. No mention of an embalmer sitting on the committee of examiners.
Licensed embalmers take part only as assessors for the oral and practical exam. By contrast, the board that licenses nurses is made up of nurses.
Counting embalmers
The number of active, licensed embalmers in the country is hard to pin down.
The DOH-CEUE has not formally published updated figures in recent years, according to PCAS. The embalmers association recorded about 5,000 licensed embalmers in 2018, though that count includes those who have died, moved abroad, or let their licenses lapse.
Exams were suspended in 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Since resumption, each exam has licensed roughly 100 people, bringing the total to between 6,000 and 6,300, according to the embalmers association. PCAS estimates 200 to 300 new embalmers a year.
In March 2026, 75 aspirants earned their licenses. After the September 2026 written exam, 125 moved on to the oral and practical portion.
Better data would help as Singapore, Malaysia, and employers in the Middle East, Europe, and North America look to hire Filipino embalmers, Ovejera said.
“Without knowing the actual figures…we don’t even know: do we have enough [at home]?” Ovejera said.
The counts also miss a group that’s harder to track: people who embalm without a license, which DOH rules prohibit. Several embalmers we spoke with said the practice persists, particularly in provinces where training is inaccessible.
Room to grow
Both men remain hopeful that the industry will continue to catch up.
For Cribello, the work remains “the ultimate noble cause.” In his classes, he pushes the fundamentals of hygiene and care for grieving families, along with sounder business practices for a new generation of operators.
“While it’s [grim] and tiring, it gives fulfillment that I can have a platform where I can influence not just one student, but operators and embalmers all throughout the country,” he said.
For Ovejera, it became all the more personal in 2023, when his father died. “I wanted to make sure that we do the best for him,” he said. He helped embalm his father himself.
That experience, he said, further strengthened the importance of the work to grieving families. “The picture of an individual lying there inside the casket…will always be in the cognitive footprint of the family members,” he said.
PEAP has also explored ladderized programs through the introduction of embalming into more Filipino universities, Ovejera said. For now, it remains a short certificate course rather than a degree.
“There’s a lot more work to do… We want to be more globally competitive,” he said. – Rappler.com

title: [New Rx] What if the Philippines leased an island for 100 years?
content:
The Philippine peso recently reached a record low of ₱64.17 against the US dollar. While currency depreciation alone does not indicate economic weakness, it raises a key question: how can the Philippines strengthen investor confidence and attract long-term capital for economic transformation?
During a visit to the Philippines, my father made an unusual suggestion: why not lease one island to another country for 100 years?
Under this proposal, the partner country would help establish a distinct legal and institutional framework while the Philippines retains sovereignty, national defense, and responsibility for essential public services. After a century, the Philippines would inherit a thriving economic center with modern infrastructure and competitive institutions.
An idea with an unexpected precedent
In January 2016, then-presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte proposed leasing islands to multinational companies with autonomy to develop infrastructure and operating rules. However, my father’s proposal differs: rather than relying on private corporations, it involves a government-to-government institutional partnership.
The historical comparison is Hong Kong. In 1898, China leased the New Territories to Britain for 99 years. Decades later, Hong Kong helped channel international capital, expertise, and commerce into Shenzhen and the Pearl River Delta, illustrating how a jurisdiction with distinct institutions can stimulate development far beyond its borders.
Not another economic zone
The Philippines already offers investment incentives and special economic zones, but these remain subject to the national administrative framework. What if one island operated under a distinct system of civil and commercial laws, an independent judiciary, taxation, and regulatory institutions?
The goal would be to offer investors predictable rules, enforceable contracts, and credible institutions. Like Hong Kong, it could feature separate residency arrangements while preserving Philippine citizenship.
Importantly, the foreign partner would not operate the entire government. The Philippines would continue providing healthcare, education, policing, municipal services, and defense. The partner would supply the institutional architecture: judicial expertise, regulatory standards, and independent oversight.
Such an arrangement would require constitutional changes, particularly to establish an independent judiciary and a distinct immigration system. The experiment would concern institutions, not merely financial incentives.
Why would Singapore be interested?
Singapore’s domestic market is small, land and labor are constrained, and its companies need international expansion. Initiatives like the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone demonstrate its strategy of pairing financial and technological strengths with regional land and workforce capacity.
A Philippine island could offer another variation of that strategy. Singaporean businesses could establish manufacturing facilities, logistics hubs, and research campuses operating under familiar standards. Headquarters and advanced research would remain in Singapore, while land-intensive operations locate on the island.
Unlike conventional industrial parks, the arrangement would feature a separate judicial and regulatory framework supported by Singaporean institutions.
Private investors could finance much of the infrastructure, limiting Singaporean taxpayer exposure while Singapore contributes institutional expertise rather than assuming territorial administration. Singapore has not expressed interest in such an arrangement, and its potential participation would require further examination.
South Korea offers another possibility
Alternatively, South Korea brings strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and digital governance. The partner could be any country with strong institutions, proven administrative capabilities, and no territorial ambitions.
An economic engine for surrounding provinces
Imagine an underdeveloped island transformed into an international commercial center with modern ports, industrial parks, and universities. The benefits would extend to surrounding provinces supplying agriculture, labor, and materials, stimulating investment across the region. Any location would require an independent feasibility study and a credible process for securing the informed consent of affected communities.
Protecting sovereignty — and the foreign partner
To protect Philippine sovereignty, foreign military bases and territorial claims would be prohibited. The Philippines would retain national defense and natural resource rights, while existing residents’ citizenship, property rights, and political representation would be protected. Equally important, foreign partners would need assurances against unilateral termination by future Philippine administrations. A constitutionally authorized bilateral treaty, international arbitration, compensation provisions, and political-risk insurance could reduce these risks, although no legal safeguard could entirely eliminate them.
Could one island change expectations?
Beyond economics, experiencing predictable permits, efficient dispute resolution, and transparent rules could raise public expectations for governance across the Philippines, encouraging broader national reforms. The island’s greatest legacy might be changing what Filipinos expect from the government.
Beyond defending the peso
The Philippines has pursued growth through incentives and economic zones for decades. The next experiment should focus on institutional credibility. By starting with just one island, the Philippines could create a model that delivers capital, infrastructure, and institutional learning for generations to come. After 100 years, the Philippines could inherit not only a thriving economic center but also institutions and practices worth adopting elsewhere.
Speaking in Parliament in 1977 about Singapore’s need to develop its own institutional approach, then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew expressed a philosophy that remains relevant far beyond its original context:
“We have got to find our own style. We have got to be bold enough to experiment.” – Rappler.com
Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

content:
The past week thrilled liberals and leftists across the world as elections in three polarized countries stemmed the march of the far-right in Latin America, demonstrated student power in Europe, and humbled Benjamin Netanyahu.
These polls have been hard fought, but the post-election transitions will be doubly harder.
- Crying fraud but also facing corruption charges back home, Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate, has fled to the US into the welcoming arms of his patron, US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro can stay in America for as long as he wants, Trump said. His father, Jair, a former president, is in jail in Brazil.
- Running on an anti-corruption wave, Serbia’s student protest movement managed to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election, but now comes the hard part of governing. For starters, the student leaders have called for the resignation of top public officials and investigations into alleged corruption under Vucic.
- In Israel, the far-right continues to dominate, but did not come out solidly for Netanyahu, whose party lost the majority in parliament. Without any bloc enjoying majority numbers, however, he will likely serve as caretaker prime minister. How could Israel break an election deadlock? Here’s an explainer.
And so we turn to the next logical question: what will America show the rest of the world this week?
The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as Trump enters the last two years of his term. Here are things to know.
If you’re a liberal and listened to pollster Nate Silver’s interview with Ezra Klein (as I did), you’d be expecting a “momentous” turnaround — a more than 70% chance for Democrats in the Senate — that could flip Congress against Trump. If the results reflect what he’s seeing in his polling, Silver said these would effectively end the Trump era.
The Economist has more conservative numbers. While conceding that the “auguries are good for Democrats,” it’s putting the probability of the US Senate going to the Democrats at just 54%. - These are the races that will decide control of the US Senate, and the key seats that could shape the next House.
- The campaign period has been reminiscent of traditional tactics in Philippine elections, writes Filipino-American Oscar Quiambao in this piece. There have been concerns about Republican efforts to delay the vote counts and intimidate voters. And let’s not forget that Trump himself offered $5,000 to every American if Republicans win.

A fake video about him supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio went viral.

title: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
content:
AT A GLANCE
- Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators regarding a proposal to end the war with the United States, with a follow-up meeting possible.
- The discussions are based on a seven-step plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade, with Iran suggesting a faster implementation timeline.
- Iran's demands include the end of the US blockade and respect for its requirements, while concerns about potential conflict escalation remain amid the upcoming US midterm elections.
Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday, November 2.
The negotiators departed on Sunday, November 1, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the draft proposal.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran, with Tehran now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal.
The spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha to facilitate the exchange of messages with Washington via Qatari intermediaries.
“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently. These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said.
On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged.
Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump.
The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.”
Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action.

title: Senate majority united in stripping 2027 budget bill of ‘corruption-prone items’ – Lacson
content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Senate majority bloc is united in removing “corruption-prone” items from the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said.
“The majority of senators are rallying behind Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito’s efforts to cleanse the 2027 budget of unwarranted, whimsical, and corruption-prone items — all means all!” Lacson said in a social media post.
Over the weekend, Lacson said Ejercito had secured the commitment of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) that it will submit all supporting documents for its infrastructure projects by Tuesday, November 3. Projects without the required documents would be removed from the House-approved version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
Budget advocacy groups, including the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, had flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion with no published project attachments in the HGAB.
A separate Senate review also found that the number of DPWH projects had increased from 11,420 in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to 16,244 in the House-approved GAB. Of these, 6,271 were new projects introduced by lawmakers without prior vetting by the executive branch.
Lacson also said Ejercito would invite civil society organizations to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the budget, which would be livestreamed to promote transparency.
The Senate will take up the budget bill when plenary sessions resume on November 9, with plenary debates expected to begin on November 23. – Rappler.com

title: What does the Million Mask March mean for the Philippines?
content:
AT A GLANCE
- The Million Mask March, a global protest event held on November 5, originated from the hacking collective Anonymous and is associated with themes of political dissent and activism.
- Past events, particularly in 2013, saw significant online defacements of Philippine government websites as a precursor to the protests, highlighting issues like political corruption and police violence.
- The upcoming 2026 Million Mask March may be influenced by recent controversies within the Philippine Department of Information and Communications Technology, potentially leading to renewed protest actions.
MANILA, Philippines – If you see a defaced Philippine government website this early in November, it could be a one-off event, but it also may be a single defacement of many, owing to a movement called the Million Mask March.
The Million Mask March is a worldwide day of protest held on November 5 and is also colloquially known as “Operation Vendetta,” after the movie and British graphic novel V for Vendetta, wherein the main character of the story wears a Guy Fawkes mask.
Originally set up by hacking collective Anonymous, the Million Mask March began in 2012 with the largest events occurring outside the Philippines, such as in London in the United Kingdom and Washington DC in the United States.
The event is usually preceded by hacking activities or online defacements of websites to drum up interest and sentiment in conducting a Million Mask March in a given locality. These defacements and hacks decry a number of issues, such as political corruption, police violence and militarization.
This was most strongly felt in the early iterations of the protest, especially in the Philippines’ 2013 Million Mask March, which saw more than 30 Philippine government websites crashed or defaced.
A video from Anonymous on the affected sites back then apologized for the disruption but called on citizens to join the November 5 protest action. In response, police at the time also took steps to maintain public safety, but also invited protesters in for questioning.
An impactful Million Mask March for 2026?
Activity related to Million Mask March tends to fluctuate depending on the time frame of issues brought up.
While the 2025 Million Mask March was apparently less pronounced and did not receive as much media coverage save for notices in online hacking communities, there’s no telling what might spur on a 2026 protest action.
The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) could possibly be in for a long few days of work though, seeing as there is a new DICT secretary, former Social Security System chief Robert Joseph de Claro,.
There also seeming loss of trust in the institution owing to the actions — and resignation — of the previous DICT secretary, Henry Aguda, as regards the temporary banning of Discord and the threat to ban other services that may be responsible for the spread of nihilistic violent extremism.
There’s also the preventive suspension of DICT eGov Undersecretary David Almirol over alleged conflicts of interest in the eGov app and the system’s development, which may bring an opportunity for bad actors or hacker-activists to take advantage of the situation.
Unfortunately, there’s no telling what could spark strong protest actions on November 5 in the Philippines, and it’s just as difficult to determine if an informal Million Mask March is coming this year.
Perhaps it’s better to remember the fifth of November as a day when plans to bring injustices to the forefront of public consciousness comes to a head.
Though in this country, that may as well be any given weekday. – Rappler.com

Despite rainy weather, members and supporters of political party Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) gathered outside the Supreme Court (SC) on Tuesday morning.

'Delays'
