title: ICC prosecutors want to admit 3 pre-recorded testimonies on Duterte's 'narco-list'
content:
PRAGUE, Czech Republic – To expedite the proceedings in Rodrigo Duterte’s case before the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Office of the Prosecutor seeks to admit three pre-recorded witness testimonies regarding the former President’s “narco list.”
In a redacted request for application filed on November 2, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang requested Trial Chamber III to admit the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-1097, P-1170, and P-1318, which are “relevant” proof of Duterte’s “individual criminal liability”, particularly in identifying “high-value targets” on various drug watch lists.
The prosecution added that these statements also establish the Philippine National Police’s (PNP) role in Duterte’s drug war.
Niang stated that the prior recorded testimonies are introduced via the ICC’s Rule of Procedure and Evidence Rule 68(3), which may allow admission of such statements in proceedings while the witness appears in court and does not object.
Recorded testimonies
Although heavily redacted, the three witnesses’ statements, as the prosecution noted, establish the targeting of individuals by PNP officers during Duterte’s drug war, as well as “the shift in [REDACTED] after Mr Duterte became President.”
P-1097’s prior recorded testimony explains the “tokhang” killings and that “warning placards were placed on some victims.”
The prosecution noted that P-1170’s testimony demonstrates Duterte’s public accusation of redacted individuals as being involved with illegal drugs, who were later included on the “PRRD list.”
The pre-recorded testimony of P-1318 is heavily redacted, but the prosecution said it describes the Operation Double Barrel and the tokhang killings, including “some police killings [that] were staged through nanlaban narratives, evidence planting, and cover-ups.”
The prosecution noted that it would conduct a “limited and focused supplementary examination” of the witnesses – all referred to in the filing with male pronouns – should their prior recorded testimonies be introduced as evidence.
It also seeks to use associated materials for P-1097, P-1170, and P-1318 as evidence “necessary to fully comprehend” their accounts.
The filing noted that the three witnesses’ statements “are internally consistent, mutually corroborative, and accompanied by supporting documents in relation to certain aspects,” and that they corroborate the evidence to be provided by other viva voce witnesses.
'Paper-only' witness
Meanwhile, Duterte’s defense counsel, Peter Haynes, is asking Trial Chamber III to reject the prosecution’s application to admit witness P-1357’s prior recorded testimony under Rule 68(2), which would allow the statement in court without the witness’s appearance.
In a redacted response filing on the same day, Haynes claims P-1357 “exemplifies the very type of individual whom the Chamber urged the Prosecution to remove from its list.”
“Her testimony is entirely peripheral, as it does not address the substance of [REDACTED] research, the allegations made, or the findings reached. The witness is not even familiar with the events occurring after [REDACTED], having ceased working on the subject following [REDACTED],” Haynes stated.
It may be recalled that the prosecution asked Trial Chamber III on October 19 to admit the prior recorded testimony of P-1357, P-0024, and P-1359 as Rule 68(2)(b) evidence that relates to the alleged systematic policy of “neutralizing” alleged criminals across the Philippines through murder.
The prior recorded testimony of P-1357, referred to in female pronouns, contains details of the existence and operations of the Davao Death Squad and “notes that the words and actions of Mr Duterte indicated his support for killings of criminal suspects.”
But Haynes objected to admitting P-1357’s statement, saying it “adds nothing of substance to the evidence in this case.”
“Further and/or alternatively, the Defence objects to the Prosecution’s improper use of Rule 68(2)(b) to introduce associated material that the witness has neither meaningfully used nor explained, contrary to the Prosecution’s assertions,” Haynes stated.
Haynes said the defense has “no wish” to cross-examine P-1357, “given the marginal relevance of her testimony.”
The defense said it won’t cross-examine P-0024 because of “having already extensively addressed its concerns regarding the introduction of the [REDACTED] dataset into the evidentiary record of these proceedings.”
P-0024’s heavily redacted statement mentions a “legal process,” and “records [that] may have been incomplete or selectively disclosed.” It remains unclear which information P-0024’s statement refers to.
Ramifications, deadlines
At the final status conference, senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls and trial lawyer Edward Jeremy told Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner that the Office of the Prosecution would submit eight additional applications to admit Rule 68(3) witnesses.
Korner also asked the prosecution and the defense for suggestions on in-court protective measures regarding Rule 68(3) witnesses, citing “various ramifications” and the need for “certainty about the deadlines.”
Earlier, Nichols said that by submitting prior recorded witness statements, they hope to “cut down in half” the six hours allocated to present their opening statements.
The ICC’s trial of Duterte for crimes against humanity is set for November 30. —VAL, GMA News

title: EXPLAINER: ICC Rules 68.2 and 68.3: How prior witness testimonies may be used in Duterte trial
content:
THE HAGUE — Rules 68.2 and 68.3 of the International Criminal Court's (ICC) Rules of Procedure and Evidence were mentioned during the fifth and final status conference in the case of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte on Monday.
The provisions concern the use of previously recorded witness testimony and this could affect how evidence is presented when Duterte's trial begins on November 30.
The key distinction between the two rules is whether the witness must appear before the Trial Chamber.
Under Rule 68.2, the court may allow previously recorded testimony to be introduced even if the witness is not present. This is permitted only under specific circumstances, including when both the prosecution and defense had the opportunity to examine the witness during the recording, or when the witness has died, is unavailable despite reasonable efforts, or has been subjected to improper interference.
The rule also allows the introduction of testimony concerning matters other than the accused's acts and conduct, subject to additional requirements.
Rule 68.3, meanwhile, applies when the witness is present before the Trial Chamber. Previously recorded testimony may be introduced if the witness does not object and the prosecution, defense and judges have the opportunity to examine them during the proceedings.
Atty. Kristina Conti, an ICC counsel representing the victims, explained that Rule 68.3 covers witnesses who already have recorded statements or other material on record.
“Ang ibig sabihin lang po nito, ang may 68.3, ito po ay mga witnesses na meron ng dating testimonya, dokumento o, ah, videos na sila'y nagsasalaysay. So kumbaga may affidavit na dati,” Conti said.
(What this means is that the 68.3 are witnesses who have previous testimonies, documents or, ah, videos of them giving their accounts. So there was an affidavit before.)
Conti said the existence of these materials could help shorten court proceedings because some of the witness's statements and supporting evidence have already been documented.
“Si 68.3, sisipot pa rin (68.3 will still show up),” she said, stressing that witnesses under this provision would still appear before the court.
For Rule 68.2, Conti explained: “Si 68.2, replacement of the testimony. Tanggapin yung testimonya nila pero hindi nasisipot yung witnesses (Their testimony is accepted but they will not appear).”
The use of previously recorded testimony may, however, be contested by the defense, which has raised concerns about its ability to question witnesses whose evidence is significant to the prosecution's case.
The defense has also pointed to the need to examine how certain reports and documents were produced, including the people involved in preparing them. It has indicated that it intends to present its own witnesses in response to the prosecution's evidence.
The Trial Chamber will ultimately decide whether a particular recorded testimony can be admitted under Rule 68 and whether the requirements have been met.
Duterte's trial is scheduled to begin on November 30. — BAP, GMA News

title: Duterte ICC trial: Victims face language barriers, concerns over scope of charges
content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands — Victims of alleged crimes committed during former president Rodrigo Duterte's war on drugs face challenges in participating meaningfully in his upcoming trial before the International Criminal Court (ICC), including language barriers, witness protection concerns, and questions over the scope of charges.
Among the key concerns raised during the court's fifth status conference on Monday, November 2, was an ICC decision that could limit the killings covered by the case, potentially excluding some victims from the proceedings.
The conference also addressed preparations for Duterte's trial, scheduled to open on November 30, including witness protection measures and arrangements for victims' participation.
In an interview, attorney Kristina Conti, an ICC Assistant to Counsel, said these issues remain significant for victims as the proceedings approach.
Change in scope of charges raises concerns for victims
Conti said victims' representatives are grappling with the implications of an ICC decision issued on October 9 that appears to limit the scope of killings covered by one of the charges.
The case concerns alleged crimes committed between November 1, 2011, and March 16, 2019, when the Philippines was a member of the ICC. However, the decision reportedly limits the killings covered by one charge to the period between July 1, 2016, and September 30, 2018.
“Yung tinatawag na paglimita ng scope ang problema ngayon ng mga biktima kasi posibleng hindi lahat, eh, pumasok doon sa parameters,” Conti told GMA News Online.
(The limitation of the scope is now a problem for victims because some of them may not fall within the parameters of the case.)
Conti said victims' representatives are still trying to understand the implications of the ruling, arguing that the alleged crimes should be considered within the full period of the Philippines' membership in the ICC.
“Dapat hanggang 2019 na miyembro yung Pilipinas ng ICC. Tapos dapat hanggang 2022 kung kailan tsaka pa lang natapos yung term ni Duterte,” she said.
(It should cover when the Philippines was a member of the ICC, until 2019. And Duterte's term only ended in 2022.)
The potential narrowing of the scope is a concern for victims who fear that not all alleged crimes may be considered in the proceedings.
Participating victims need not testify
Conti clarified that victims participating in the proceedings do not necessarily have to take the witness stand. Their role is to express their views and concerns through their common legal representatives and, potentially, seek reparations if Duterte is convicted.
She stressed that the number of participating victims does not determine the strength of the prosecution's evidence.
“Yung pagliit o paglaki ng bilang na ito ay hindi nakakaapekto directly doon sa kaso or doon sa strength ng evidence. Pero siyempre, ibang tulong din yun na alam ng prosecution, makikita nila na ganito karami ang gustong mag-participate,” she said.
(The increase or decrease in the number of participating victims does not directly affect the case or the strength of the evidence. But, of course, it also helps the prosecution to see how many people want to participate.)
Conti encouraged victims to participate even if they are unwilling or unable to testify, submit affidavits, or recount their experiences in court.
“Pero gusto pa rin sana namin na anyayahan sila na mag-participate. Not necessarily para maging witness, not necessarily para magbigay ng statement na kumbaga affidavit, pero para magbigay ng views and concerns, mga pananaw at mga agam-agam,” she said.
(We still want to encourage them to participate. Not necessarily as witnesses, and not necessarily to submit affidavits, but to share their views and concerns.)
Applications from participating victims will continue to be accepted until the prosecution finishes presenting its evidence, Conti said.
The prosecution has been allotted 150 hours to present its evidence, a phase she estimates could take approximately a year.
Victims' safety and participation
Conti said preparations for the November 30 trial were largely in place, with the court emphasizing protective measures for witnesses who will testify either in person or through audio-visual links.
“Pero yung maganda nga dito na na-emphasize ay yung protective measures para sa witnesses,” she said.
(What was particularly good was the emphasis on protective measures for witnesses.)
These measures could include withholding witnesses' identities and preventing them from appearing on screen if the ICC determines that revealing their identities could put them at risk.
“Posibleng hindi rin natin makita sa screen. Posibleng boses lang ang marinig natin o kaya translated voice,” said Conti.
(We may not even see them on screen. We may hear only their voice, or a translated voice.)
She said protecting victims and witnesses is particularly important given the trauma they may experience when recounting alleged abuses.
Filipino language request faces hurdles
Another issue raised by victims' representatives was the request to use Filipino during portions of the proceedings, particularly when reading statements directly from victims.
Conti said the request was not simply about language preference but about allowing victims to hear their experiences conveyed in their own words.
“Hindi sila magsasalita ng Tagalog simple dahil gusto nila, kundi dahil meron silang i-quote o babasahin na statement diretso directly from the victims,” she said.
(They are not asking to speak in Tagalog simply because they want to, but because they intend to quote or read statements directly from the victims.)
However, the request appears unlikely to be granted, meaning statements would have to be delivered in English or translated.
Conti said this would not affect the legal merits of the case but could influence victims' perception of whether they are genuinely included in the proceedings.
“Pero yung impression lang sa Pilipinas, yung participation ng victims. Kumbaga eh, isinali niyo na nga kami... Pero kailangan pala English dito,” she said.
(But it affects the impression in the Philippines about victims' participation. It's as if we're being told, ‘You've included us, but everything has to be in English.’)
She warned that the English-language requirement could discourage some victims from participating, particularly those without immediate access to lawyers or legal representatives.
“Isa siyang malaking barrier—lalo na sa iba na hindi naman naaabot kaagad nung CLRV o kaya nakakapag-consult agad sa mga abogado, so baka maiwan sila sa proseso o hindi nila maintindihan ang nangyayari.”
(It is a significant barrier, especially for those who cannot immediately reach a common legal representative or consult a lawyer. They could be left behind in the process or may not understand what is happening.)
Duterte's trial is scheduled to begin on November 30. He faces three counts of crimes against humanity in connection with alleged killings during his administration's anti-drug campaign. — BM, GMA News

title: PH, Indonesia seek to deepen ties under 5-year action plan
content:
The Philippines and Indonesia reaffirmed their commitment to boost bilateral ties, including cooperation on maritime security, economic relations and border management.
Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro and Indonesia's new Foreign Minister Arrmanatha “Tata” Christiawan Nasir met in Manila on Monday during the Indonesian diplomat's introductory visit following his appointment as the country's top diplomat last month, the DFA said.
The two officials discussed progress in bilateral relations, citing the Philippines and Indonesia's historical, cultural and geographical ties as maritime neighbors and founding members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
They also recalled the outcomes of the 8th Joint Commission on Bilateral Cooperation held in Jakarta on April 23, 2026, and reaffirmed their commitment to strengthen cooperation in political and economic affairs, maritime security, border management, boundary delimitation, legal and consular matters, development in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), and people-to-people relations.
The two foreign ministers agreed to expedite the adoption of a new five-year Philippines-Indonesia Plan of Action to serve as a framework for further strengthening their partnership and advancing regional peace, stability and prosperity.
They also exchanged views on regional and global issues, particularly within ASEAN and the United Nations, including efforts to address transboundary haze and make meaningful progress on the situation in Myanmar.
Lazaro likewise welcomed Indonesia's continued support for the Philippines' ASEAN chairship ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit this month.
Both officials underscored their shared commitment to preserving ASEAN unity and centrality in addressing regional challenges. —LDF, GMA News

title: P459B worth of DPWH projects awarded to firms with questionable capacity —COA
content:
The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged 11,391 Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) projects worth P459 billion, which were awarded to contractors with questionable financial capacity.
"Review of the 27,094 sampled infrastructure contracts disclosed that 11,391 contracts with an aggregate contract cost of P459.262 billion involved bidders whose submitted Statements of Ongoing Government and Private Contracts did not completely reflect their ongoing and awarded but not yet stated contractual commitments," according to a COA Audit Report quoted on a "24 Oras" report by Maki Pulido.
"The incomplete declaration of ongoing contractual commitments resulted in Net Financial Contracting Capacity (NFCC) computations that did not fully consider the bidders’ outstanding obligations, thereby overstating their available contracting capacity and affecting the reliability of financial eligibility assessments during the post-disqualification," the COA report added.
The report said that 198 contractors should not have been given additional contracts because their previous contracts have not been completed.
"Audit disclosed that 198 contractors awarded to certain contractors in DPWH North Manila DEO in NCR initially met the NFCC requirements during the preliminary examination of bids. However, the same contractors were subsequently awarded multiple contracts under the Early Procurement Activities," COA said.
"When these contracts were considered collectively, the contractors’ remaining NFCC was no longer sufficient to cover the cumulative ABCs, indicating that their available contracting capacity had been exhausted," it added.
The incomplete declaration of ongoing contractual commitments resulted in Net Financial Contracting Capacity (NFCC) computations that did not fully consider the bidders’ outstanding obligations, thereby overstating their available contracting capacity and affecting the reliability of financial eligibility assessments during the post disqualification.
One of the contractors was awarded four more contracts worth P530 million, even though it should have been eligible to take on only P81 million worth of projects.
Another contractor secured seven contracts worth P1 billion, despite being eligible to take on only P189 million worth of projects.
According to the COA report, the following regions recorded the highest number of contracts awarded to bidders with incomplete documentary requirements:
- Region I – 1,893 contracts worth P45.76 billion
- Region X – 1,328 contracts worth P63.55 billion
- Region IV-A – 1,289 contracts worth P41.65 billion
- Region II – 1,213 contracts worth P43.55 billion
- Region III – 1,134 contracts worth P40.28 billion
MIMAROPA (Region IV-B) had the highest total value of contracts awarded to bidders with incomplete documents, at P65.70 billion across 419 contracts.
The DPWH said it validated the contractors' Net Financial Contracting Capacity (NFCC) during the post-qualification stage. It explained that the projects had not yet been awarded when the contractors submitted their bids, so these were not included in the NFCC computation.
The COA, however, said the DPWH may review bidders' qualifications at any stage of the procurement process.
The DPWH also had information that the contractors had already secured other projects, which could serve as grounds for reassessing their capacity to take on additional contracts.
“The findings of the COA in their Audit Observation Memoranda covering prior years are forwarded to the concerned Implementing Office so they can address the same. We shall coordinate with the IOs on the status of their compliance and will share an update once we have their responses,” said DPWH Secretary Giovanni Lopez.
GMA News has sought comment from former DPWH chiefs Manuel Bonoan and Vince Dizon, but has yet to receive a response. —LDF, GMA News

title: ICC adopts 1-hour trial blocks with 30-minute breaks for Duterte trial
content:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has adopted a trial schedule of one-hour blocks separated by 30-minute breaks for the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, acting on expert advice.
Trial Chamber III adopted the modified sitting schedule during the fifth and final status conference for the case, held at the ICC in The Hague on Monday.
Duterte was not present after the court granted a defense request excusing him from the proceeding.
“In order to accommodate what the experts advised in respect to Mr. Duterte, we'll run now from 10 [a.m.] to 11 [a.m.], 11:30 [a.m.] to 12:30 [p.m.],” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said.
“There will be a one-hour break for lunch… But I think this is necessary because of the circumstances of the case to keep those breaks and also finish at a time which allows everybody to deal with matters outside the trial,” she added.
In a decision made public on October 8, Trial Chamber III found Duterte fit to stand trial and instructed the ICC Registry to make necessary arrangements for the court proceedings.
Among the measures recommended by the Registry was a sitting schedule organized into one-hour blocks.
Under the adopted schedule, Duterte’s trial proceedings are expected to run from 10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., resume from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and break for lunch from 12:30 p.m. to 1:30 p.m.
Trial proceedings will resume from 1:30 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. and will continue following the same pattern of one-hour sessions separated by 30-minute breaks.
The trial proper in the case against Duterte is set to open on November 30, 2026. — BM, GMA News

title: ICC rejects victims' request to use Tagalog in parts of opening statement in Duterte trialThe International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III that will hear the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has rejected the counsel for the victims' request that portions of their opening statement be delivered in Tagalog.GMA News Online
content:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III that will hear the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has rejected the counsel for the victims' request that portions of their opening statement be delivered in Tagalog.
This was one of the measures that the trial chamber decided in its fifth pre-trial conference at the ICC in The Hague. Duterte was not present at the conference on Monday after the court granted the defense's request that he not attend.
Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said allowing Tagalog—which is not among the ICC’s official languages—would complicate victim applications and significantly increase trial costs because of translation requirements.
“One of the problems is the moment we start doing this, then applications come, and it becomes much more complicated and more expensive if we accede to it," Korner said.
"So while we understand that… you want the victims to relate to what's being said, all of it, as I understand it, is that correct, will be translated in any event, interpreted?” Korner said.
“I’m afraid, as I say for a number of reasons, we’re going to follow what the Rome Statute has mandated, and it must all be in English,” Korner said.
The request was raised by Massidda, who argued that using Tagalog was necessary to accurately convey the victims' narratives.
Massida noted that the use of Tagalog would be strictly limited to quoting victims and would not be used throughout the entire opening statement.
“We are not requesting to speak for one hour in Tagalog. Our request is more during the opening statement; we will make some remarks in quoting parts of [the] narrative that victims provided to us, and we’d like to do that in Tagalog,” Massidda explained.
“For them, it is important to listen out, convey to the Chamber what they narrated to us, and, by experience, they relate and connect much more if that is done in Tagalog,” she added.
In her estimation, Massidda said the use of Tagalog in their opening statement was expected to last no more than 15 to 20 minutes.
Under the Rome Statute, the official languages of the ICC are English and French.
Meanwhile, during the status conference, Duterte’s defense counsel, Peter Haynes, expressed that he also intends to deliver a statement at the start of the case.
“I’m inclined to say something at the start of the case. We will certainly finalize that position within the next few days,” Haynes said. –NB, GMA News

title: BI nabs alleged JP Dragon crime syndicate leader in Cabanatuan
content:
A Japanese fugitive, reportedly among the leaders of the transnational criminal syndicate JP Dragon, was arrested during an operation in Cabanatuan City on October 31, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) said Sunday.
The bureau identified the Japanese citizen as 57-year-old Yamamoto Yoshitama, who is wanted in Japan for fraud, theft, and attempted theft under an arrest warrant issued by the Fukuoka Summary Court on December 27, 2022.
According to BI Fugitive Search Unit Chief Rendel Ryan Sy, Yamamoto was allegedly among the leaders of JP Dragon, a Japan-based criminal syndicate "composed largely of former yakuza members and believed to operate primarily in Metro Manila."
“The group has been linked to sophisticated telephone fraud schemes targeting elderly Japanese citizens. Its members allegedly impersonate police officers to deceive victims into surrendering their ATM cards and banking information,” BI said.
“Japanese investigators suspect that the syndicate defrauded approximately 250 victims of around ¥900 million (around Php362 million) since 2019,” it added.
Yamamoto is expected to be held at the BI Warden’s Facility while awaiting deportation proceedings.
Immigration Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said the Philippines will not be a "safe haven" for foreign fugitives, adding that the bureau will ensure the country's borders remain secure against international criminals seeking refuge.
The BI said it remains committed to sustaining its operations against foreign fugitives and maintaining close coordination with local and international law enforcement agencies. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

title: Rodrigo Duterte's final ICC status conference set ahead of November trialThe International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III is set to hold its fifth and final status conference on Monday for the case against former President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, ahead of the start of his trial proper on November 30, 2026.GMA News Online
content:
The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III is set to hold its fifth and final status conference on Monday for the case against former President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, ahead of the start of his trial proper on November 30, 2026.
During the status conference, the court is expected to discuss key procedural preparations for the upcoming trial.
The session is scheduled to run from 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. (5 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Philippine time), with an additional session set from 12 p.m. to 1:30 p.m. (7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m.), if needed.
The hearing will be broadcast on a 30-minute delay via the ICC’s official website and social media accounts.
For this final status conference, Trial Chamber III and the parties are expected to tackle the following:
- Daily sitting schedule
- Audio-Visual Link testimony and Rights of Audience
- List of Witnesses
- Number of hours for the Prosecution's presentation of evidence
- Potentially Exculpatory Evidence, agreed facts and calling order
- Rule 68(3) applications and in-court protective measures
- Security of Defence missions
According to a document released Friday, Duterte will not attend the fifth status conference after being granted leave by Trial Chamber III. He will instead be represented by his lawyers. —LDF, GMA News

title: PNP: Over 40.7M visitors recorded in cemeteries nationwide so far for Undas 2026
content:
An estimated 40.7 million people visited cemeteries, memorial parks, and columbaria nationwide from October 30 to November 2 amid the observance of Undas 2026, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said Monday.
“Based on the nationwide monitoring report, an estimated 40,740,246 visitors had been recorded in 5,311 cemeteries, memorial parks, and columbaria from October 30 to November 2, as of 6:00 AM on November 2,” the PNP said in a statement.
“Of this figure, 1,695,440 visitors were recorded during the November 2 monitoring period as of 6 a.m.,” it added.
The PNP said it continues to sustain its nationwide security operations to ensure the safety of families visiting their departed loved ones on All Souls' Day.
Police personnel remain deployed in cemeteries and other major convergence areas to assist visitors, manage crowds, maintain peace and order, and respond to public safety concerns.
Meanwhile, authorities have confiscated a total of 6,499 prohibited items nationwide including the following:
- 879 pointed or bladed weapons
- 62 alcoholic drinks
- 2,817 lighters
- 1,739 cigarette and vape products
- 180 cooking materials
- 397 flammable substances
The PNP said its deployment is supported by personnel from other government agencies and community force multipliers, with police assistance desks and emergency response teams positioned to help visitors.
PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. reminded the public to remain vigilant, secure their personal belongings, keep children within sight, and follow cemetery regulations.
"Alam naming mahalaga ang araw na ito sa bawat pamilyang Pilipino. Kaya habang inaalala ninyo ang inyong mga mahal sa buhay, narito ang inyong kapulisan upang tumulong at tiyaking ligtas ang inyong pagdalaw,” Nartatez said.
(We know this day is important to every Filipino family. So as you remember your loved ones, your police force is here to help and ensure your visit is safe.)
“Hindi lamang kami nakabantay sa seguridad; handa rin kaming umalalay sa sinumang nangangailangan," he added.
(We are not only on guard for security, we are also ready to assist anyone in need.)
November 1 (All Saints' Day) and November 2 (All Souls' Day) were earlier declared as special non-working days to allow people to visit the tombs of their departed loved ones as part of tradition. — RSJ, GMA News

title: MNLF denies protecting Bato dela Rosa
content:
The Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) denied speculations that it is coddling embattled Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is believed to be under the protection of an “armed and powerful group.”
In a statement posted by the office of MNLF Chairman Muslimin Sema on Facebook on Sunday, the organization said that it has “no established formal relationship” with dela Rosa, and that its founder, Nur Misuari, is only a known “friend” of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
“The claim that the MNLF may be protecting him is speculation, not a confirmed fact,” the organization said.
“Dela Rosa appears to have personal and political connections to figures associated with the MNLF, especially through Duterte’s relationship with Nur Misuari, but there is no verified evidence that he is an MNLF member, ally in an operational sense, or currently being protected by the group,” it added.
The MNLF, however, cited reports that say that its organization is “fragmented” and that whether the Misuari faction would or could shield dela Rosa from arrest is “uncertain.”
It also cited claims that dela Rosa and Misuari may personally know each other, considering the latter’s ties with Duterte.
The Department of the Interior and Local Government has raised a P50-million reward for the arrest of dela Rosa, who according to Interior Secretary Juanito Victor "Jonvic" Remulla is now considered "armed and dangerous."
Remulla earlier said authorities were also negotiating with a group protecting the senator to secure his surrender and prevent a potentially violent confrontation.
The MNLF said that dela Rosa only publicly discussed their organization mainly in the context of conflict and peacebuilding.
“As a student in Marawi, he experienced fighting between government forces and the MNLF, and he has supported programs benefiting former combatants and their children,” the MNLF said.
“He has also advocated faster integration of qualified MILF and MNLF members into the PNP and AFP, indicating policy-level engagement rather than a personal or organizational tie,” it added.
GMA News Online reached out to the office of dela Rosa for a comment and will update this story once it responds.
Dela Rosa has been issued an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in relation to the drug war of Duterte, which supposedly killed thousands of people. He was chief of the Philippine National Police at the time the war on drugs was implemented.
Duterte is already detained at the ICC in The Hague, Netherlands, while awaiting his crimes against humanity trial. —KG, GMA News

title: US envoy reaffirms PH alliance 'stronger than ever' after ASEAN defense meet
content:
United States Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton on Monday reaffirmed Washington’s commitment to Philippine security, describing it as “ironclad” and the two countries’ alliance as “stronger than ever.”
Lipton issued the statement following the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus in Cebu, which was attended by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
“I want to reaffirm the United States’ enduring commitment to the Philippines and our shared vision for a peaceful, secure, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Lipton said.
He said Hegseth’s frequent engagements with Southeast Asian partners demonstrate the Trump administration’s “determination to strengthen alliances, deepen regional cooperation, and ensure that peace is backed by strength.”

Lipton added that the visits of the US Secretary of War also underscore the importance Washington places on Southeast Asia and its alliance with the Philippines.
“Our commitment to Philippine security is ironclad. With President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., the United States and the Philippines have built a powerful partnership grounded in shared principles, mutual respect, and an unwavering commitment to regional stability,” Lipton said.
“As we mark 75 years of the US-Philippines Mutual Defense Treaty, our message is clear: our alliance is stronger than ever,” he added.
Lipton also emphasized Washington’s long-term commitment to the partnership, particularly its support for defending Philippine sovereignty, protecting the country’s territorial integrity, and upholding freedom of navigation.
Beyond defense cooperation, the US envoy said the security partnership should be matched by an equally strong economic relationship, stressing Washington’s support for the Philippines’ economic development.
“The United States is proud to call the Philippines an ally, partner, and friend. Our relationship is not simply a matter of treaties or shared strategic interests; it is a bond between our peoples that grows stronger every day,” Lipton said.

title: End of Sara Duterte impeachment trial 'possible' in November, says prosecutionThe impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte could wrap up by the end of November if the defense presents its evidence within 10 full trial days, House lead prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said.
content:
The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte could wrap up by the end of November if the defense presents its evidence within 10 full trial days, House lead prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said.
In a statement, Luistro raised the possibility after the House prosecution panel on October 13 dropped three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte, which covered allegations of misuse of confidential funds, bribery and grave threats.
The defense team had originally sought 30 trial days to present its evidence on all four Articles of Impeachment under the pretrial order.
“Posible po na matapos ito bago ang katapusan ng Nobyembre,” Luistro said.
(It’s possible that the trial will conclude before the end of November.)
“We have reason to believe na ito pong 30 trial days na ito ay malaki ang mababawas. Sana kalahati na lang o sampu na lang,” she added.
(We have reason to believe that these 30 trial days will be significantly reduced. Hopefully, only half or 10 days will be needed.)
Luistro, however, said the final trial schedule would remain subject to the approval of the Senate impeachment court and the number of witnesses the defense intends to present.
If the defense requires more than the expected 10 full trial days, the proceedings could extend into December.
“But at any rate, we are all hoping and praying na sana naman bago mag-Pasko ay tapos na ang impeachment trial na ito para magkaroon tayo ng closure, and we can all move on,” Luistro said.
(But at any rate, we are all hoping and praying that the impeachment trial will be over before Christmas so we can have closure, and we can all move on.)
The impeachment trial is currently suspended to give way to Senate committee deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.
The Senate impeachment court is scheduled to reconvene on November 9 at 10 a.m.
'Dilatory tactics'
Luistro also said the defense could resort to dilatory tactics when the trial resumes, such as filing a demurrer to evidence or insisting on presenting evidence related to the three Articles of Impeachment that the prosecution had withdrawn.
“But our position on that is, kung iniurong na ang habla, kung wala nang sakdal, kung wala nang allegations, for what adjudicatory purpose will the presentation of the defense's evidence serve?” Luistro said in an online interview with GMA News' Sandra Aguinaldo.
(But our position on this is, if the charges have been withdrawn and there are no longer any accusations or allegations, what adjudicatory purpose would the presentation of the defense's evidence serve?)
“Wala nang kailangang sagutin, wala nang kailangang dipensahan, wala nang dahilan to present evidence with respect to the three articles withdrawn already,” she added.
(There is nothing left to answer, nothing left to defend against. There is no longer any reason to present evidence regarding the three articles that have already been withdrawn.)
Luistro said the defense might also attempt to raise matters concerning the dropped articles during the proceedings, but the prosecution would oppose such moves.
“Bagaman prerogative nila 'yan to file the proper remedy they believe will be appropriate given the situation, we're really hoping na mag-proceed sila sa presentation of evidence,” Luistro said.
(Although it is their prerogative to seek the appropriate remedy they believe is warranted under the circumstances, we are really hoping they will proceed with the presentation of evidence.)
With the decision to drop three Articles of Impeachment, the prosecution will pursue only Article II, which concerns allegations that Duterte failed to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.
Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison earlier said the move would not affect the defense panel's presentation of evidence, stressing that Duterte should still be allowed to address allegations already presented before the impeachment court.
“That prerogative to withdraw an accusation is not the power to suppress its rebuttal on the part of the respondent. The authority to streamline, or to achieve speed in a trial, is not the authority to diminish due process, or to altogether disregard fundamental rules of fairness," Sison said.
"And the desire to reach a verdict expeditiously can never justify reaching it unfairly,” she added.— MCG, GMA News

title: PH Red Cross attends to over 8,700 patients during Undas 2026
content:
The Philippine Red Cross (PRC) on Monday said it has attended to 8,721 patients nationwide since October 29 amid the observance of Undas 2026.
Based on the PRC's latest operational report as of 9 a.m. on Monday, all 8,721 patients received vital signs monitoring.
The PRC said 359 were classified as minor cases, while 19 were considered major cases.
The minor cases included dizziness, headaches, lacerations, abrasions, insect bites, difficulty breathing, sprains, burns, hypertension, fever, and injuries sustained in motorcycle crashes.
Major cases included chest pain, seizures, suspected stroke, cardiac arrest, heat stroke, and difficulty breathing.
According to the PRC, nine patients were brought to hospitals due to conditions such as stroke, body weakness, loss of consciousness, and hypoglycemia.
A total of 297 welfare assistance services were also provided, including psychological first aid, referrals, tracing services, and the distribution of hot meals and food packs.
Other forms of assistance included wheelchair services for 25 individuals, water provision for 149 people, and the distribution of information and education materials.
For its Undas operations, the PRC deployed 1,977 personnel nationwide, composed of 132 staff members and 1,845 volunteers.
Its deployed assets included 73 ambulances, 404 first aid stations, 131 welfare desks, 45 foot patrols, 32 mobile units, and other service vehicles and equipment.
Cemeteries accounted for the largest number of PRC mobilization areas with 349 deployment points nationwide. Other areas included bus terminals, highways, seaports, beaches, airports, and gas stations.
The PRC's Undas Operation 2026 runs from October 29 to November 3. — Joviland Rita/RSJ, GMA News

title: PNP conducts operation vs Bantag at Ifugao poultry farm
content:
The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Monday said an operation was conducted to arrest former Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) chief Gerald Bantag at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on Sunday.
However, Bantag was not found at the location during the operation.
“Police conducted an operation at a poultry farm in Barangay Pugol, Lamut, Ifugao on November 1 after receiving information that Bantag was hiding there and posing as a poultry worker,” the PNP said in a statement.
“However, he was not found at the location,” it added.
The PNP said it remains committed to pursuing Bantag, who is wanted over his alleged involvement in the 2022 killing of broadcaster Percival Mabasa or "Percy Lapid."
PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio C. Nartatez Jr. said authorities would continue their efforts to serve the warrant against Bantag.
“We will not allow the passage of time or repeated attempts to evade arrest to weaken our resolve. The PNP will remain relentless in pursuing those who are wanted by the law,” Nartatez said.
“Every lead will be pursued, every lawful opportunity will be acted upon, and we will not stop until they are brought before the courts to answer for the charges against them,” he added.
Nartatez described the recent operation as proof of the police force's determination to locate and arrest wanted individuals.
“This is not a setback but a proof that we remain relentless in locating and arresting him as well as other high-profile fugitives,” he said.
The PNP also called on the public to provide information that could help authorities locate Bantag and other wanted individuals.
In April 2023, a Muntinlupa Regional Trial Court court ordered the arrest of Bantag in connection with the death of Jun Villamor, the alleged middleman in the killing of broadcaster Percy Lapid in October 2022.
Bantag has denied the allegations against him.
The Department of Justice (DOJ) previously said a P2-million reward would be given for information leading to Bantag’s arrest. — RSJ, GMA News
